items.title: microsim
items.text:
microsim simulates fluorescence microscopy images. You describe a sample, a microscope, and a detector, and it calculates the photons the sample emits, the image the optics form, and the noisy digital image a camera or point detector records.

Simulated images of nucleus, mitochondria, and endoplasmic reticulum. The ground truth comes from FIB-SEM segmentations of cell jrc_hela-3 at OpenOrganelle.

items.title: What it's for
items.text:
• Ground truth for image analysis. Every simulated image comes with the exact fluorophore distribution that produced it. You can use the pairs to train or benchmark segmentation, denoising, deconvolution, or super-resolution methods.
  • Planning experiments. Ask what a different objective, filter set, fluorophore, exposure time, or detector would do to your images before you change them on the microscope.
  • Teaching. Each step of image formation can be computed and plotted on its own: absorption spectra, filter transmission, PSFs, shot noise, read noise.

items.title: How it works
items.text:
A simulation is a single Simulation object that holds every parameter. Running it takes the sample through four stages:

flowchart LR
    A["<b>Sample</b><br/>fluorophores per voxel,<br/>in a high-resolution space"] --> B["<b>Emission</b><br/>photons/s per fluorophore,<br/>per channel and wavelength"]
    B --> C["<b>Optical image</b><br/>photons/s, blurred<br/>by the PSF"]
    C --> D["<b>Digital image</b><br/>gray values, with<br/>pixelation and noise"]

Each stage has its own method, and returns a labeled xarray.DataArray that you can inspect, plot, or save. The User guide explains each stage.

items.title: A first example
items.text:
from microsim import schema as ms
from microsim.util import ortho_plot

sim = ms.Simulation(
    truth_space=ms.ShapeScaleSpace(shape=(128, 512, 512), scale=(0.02, 0.01, 0.01)),
    output_space={"downscale": 8},
    sample=ms.Sample(labels=[ms.MatsLines(density=0.5, length=30, azimuth=5)]),
    detector=ms.CameraCMOS(),
)
result = sim.run()  # (C, Z, Y, X) array of gray values
ortho_plot(result)

First simulation goes through this example line by line.

Pin your version

microsim is in early development and changes quickly. New releases may include breaking API changes, and the same parameters may produce different simulation results as the physical models are corrected and extended. If you depend on microsim for a project, pin a specific version (e.g. microsim==0.x.y) and record it alongside your results.

Issues and pull requests are welcome on GitHub.

items.title: Citing microsim
items.text:
If you use microsim in published work, please cite the software through its Zenodo record:

The Zenodo page has citation text in several formats, and a DOI for each release. Since results can differ between versions, cite the version you used.

The ground truth from OpenOrganelle and the spectra from FPbase come from other projects; if you use them, please also cite:

  • Heinrich, L. et al. "Whole-cell organelle segmentation in volume electron microscopy." Nature 599, 141–146 (2021). doi:10.1038/s41586-021-03977-3
  • Lambert, T. J. "FPbase: a community-editable fluorescent protein database." Nature Methods 16, 277–278 (2019). doi:10.1038/s41592-019-0352-8

items.title: Documentation
items.text:
The docs are built with Zensical from the Markdown files in docs/, configured in zensical.toml. The API reference is generated from the source: the api-autonav plugin makes one page per public module, and mkdocstrings renders the docstrings. Modules whose contents are documented by their package are excluded there, so that each object is documented once.

uv run --group docs zensical serve   # live preview at http://localhost:8000
uv run --group docs zensical build   # build to site/

Most figures, and the data for the interactive charts, are made by microsim when the docs are built, and are not checked in. Generate them once before previewing (this needs network access for FPbase and OpenOrganelle, and takes a few minutes the first time):

uv run --group docs python scripts/make_doc_figures.py                  # everything
uv run --group docs python scripts/make_doc_figures.py pinhole_data detector_data  # some

Images are written to docs/images/generated/ and chart data to docs/data/generated/, both ignored by git. The figures of the tutorials are made by running the code blocks of each tutorial page, so the code shown always matches the images.

Each tutorial is also published as a notebook, converted from its page by scripts/make_notebooks.py (into docs/notebooks/, also ignored by git). The notebook's first cell installs microsim from the commit the docs were built from. Run the script before a strict build, which checks the notebook links:

uv run python scripts/make_notebooks.py

items.title: Interactive charts
items.text:
The interactive charts are drawn in the browser with Observable Plot and D3, loaded from jsDelivr. A chart is a placeholder in the Markdown,

<div class="ms-chart" data-chart="spectra"></div>

and a module in docs/javascripts/charts/ with the same name. Where a chart recomputes microsim's physics (so readers can change parameters), the calculation lives in docs/javascripts/physics/, and tests/test_js_physics.py runs it in node and compares it with microsim. Run that test after changing photometry or detector code; it needs node.

items.title: API reference
items.text:
All the models used to define a simulation can be imported from microsim.schema, which is usually imported as ms:

from microsim import schema as ms

ms.Simulation, ms.Confocal, ms.CameraCMOS, ...

Every model is a pydantic model. Fields are validated when the object is created and when they are assigned, and every field that takes a model also accepts a dictionary with the same keys. Unknown fields raise an error.

The pages in this section are generated from the source code, one per public module, so they always match the installed version. Each object is documented once, in the module or subpackage that defines it; most are also importable from microsim.schema, as above. The main objects, by topic:

items.title: make_confocal_psf
items.text:
make_confocal_psf(
    nz: int,
    ex_wvl_um: float = 0.475,
    em_wvl_um: float = 0.525,
    pinhole_au: float = 1.0,
    dz: float = 0.05,
    pz: float = 0,
    nx: int = 31,
    ny: int | None = None,
    pos: tuple[float, float, float] = (0, 0, 0),
    dxy: float = 0.05,
    objective: ObjectiveKwargs
    | ObjectiveLens
    | None = None,
    sf: int = 3,
    normalize: bool | Literal["sum", "max"] = "sum",
    saturation: float = 0,
    xp: NumpyAPI | None = None,
) -> ndarray

Create a confocal PSF.

This function creates a confocal system PSF: the excitation spot times the detection PSF (the emission PSF convolved with a pinhole mask). pinhole_au is in Airy units at the emission wavelength.

If normalize is False, the result is physically scaled: the relative excitation intensity (1 at focus) times the fraction of collected emission that passes the pinhole, for a point source at each position.

saturation is the excitation saturation parameter at the focus (k * tau: the absorption rate times the excited-state lifetime). If non-zero, the relative excitation r is replaced by the relative emission of a two-level system, r / (1 + s * r).

All extra keyword arguments are passed to vectorial_psf_centered.

items.title: Settings
items.text:
Settings that affect how a simulation is computed.

Every setting can also be set with an environment variable MICROSIM_<NAME> (nested settings separated by __, e.g. MICROSIM_CACHE__WRITE=0).

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default np_backend Literal['numpy', 'torch', 'jax', 'cupy', 'auto']

Array library: "numpy", "cupy", "jax", "torch", or "auto" (CuPy if it can be imported, otherwise NumPy).

'auto' device Literal['cpu', 'gpu', 'auto']

Not used yet.

'auto' random_seed int | None

Seed for random ground truth and noise. A random seed is chosen if not given.

3783344473 cache CacheSettings

Whether to read and write the on-disk ground truth cache.

<dynamic> float_dtype dtype[floating]

Floating-point precision to use for simulations.

'float32' max_psf_radius_aus float | Literal['auto'] | None

Restrict the lateral radius of simulated PSFs to this many Airy radii (1 Airy radius = 0.61 * wavelength / NA, the radius of the Airy disk; half the Airy unit used for Confocal.pinhole_au). 'auto' (default) is our opinionated balance between speed and accuracy, aiming for ~1% RMSE (and <2% max error) relative to an untruncated PSF, which is below shot noise unless pixels collect well over ~10^4 photons. For widefield, the radius grows with the depth of the simulated volume, since out-of-focus light spreads in a cone of half-angle asin(NA/n): it is ~14 Airy radii (for the tails of the in-focus Airy pattern) plus half the radius of that cone at half the volume depth (e.g. ~17 Airy radii for a 1 um deep volume, ~27 for 5 um, at NA 1.4). For confocal, where the pinhole rejects out-of-focus light, it is 8 Airy radii. A number sets the radius directly; a too-small radius loses out-of-focus light (in a 5 um deep widefield volume, 8 Airy radii lose ~20% of it). None uses the full extent of the simulated space (most accurate, but much slower for large volumes: ~2-4x slower per sample than 'auto' at 2048x2048 pixels). The PSF is never larger than the simulated space.

'auto' spectral_bins_per_emission_channel int

Number of wavelengths to use (per channel) when simulating the optical image. By default, a single centroid wavelength is used to approximate the emission wavelength. Increasing this will make the simulation more realistic, by superposing multiple different PSFs, but will also increase memory usage and time.

1 excitation_bin_width_nm float

Maximum width (nm) of the wavelength bins used to represent the excitation light absorbed by each fluorophore, for modalities that focus the excitation (e.g. confocal). Each bin uses a separate excitation spot, so laser lines further apart than this are always simulated separately.

10 spectral_bin_threshold_percentage float

Percentage of the peak intensity to use as a threshold when binning the emission (and excitation) spectra. This is used to determine the range of wavelengths to consider when simulating the optical image. First, the spectrum is trimmed to include only relevant wavelengths (those with intensity above this threshold). Then, the spectrum is discretized into spectral_bins_per_emission_channel bins (or, for excitation, bins of at most excitation_bin_width_nm).

1

items.title: ground_truth
items.text:
ground_truth() -> DataArray

Return the ground truth data.

Returns position and quantity of fluorophores in the sample. The return array has dimensions (F, Z, Y, X). The units are fluorophores counts.

Examples:

>>> sim = Simulation(...)
>>> truth = sim.ground_truth()
>>> truth.isel(f=0).max('z').plot()  # plot max projection of first fluorophore
>>> plt.show()

items.title: filtered_emission_rates
items.text:
filtered_emission_rates(
    *, saturate: bool = True
) -> DataArray

Return the emission rates for each fluorophore in each channel.

Returns a (C, F, W) array of detected emission rates for each fluorophore in each channel, as a function of wavelength. The units are photons/s. The range of wavelengths will encompass the union of all the fluorophores' emission spectra, and the rates will be zero where the fluorophore does not emit.

These are the rates for a fluorophore at the reference illumination intensity (OpticalConfig.power): anywhere in a widefield field of view, or at the center of the excitation spot for point-scanning modalities (e.g. Confocal). If saturate is True (the default), excitation saturation at that intensity is applied.

Examples:

>>> sim = Simulation(...)
>>> rates = sim.filtered_emission_rates()
>>> rates.isel(c=0).plot.line(x='w') # plot emission of all fluors in channel 0
>>> plt.show()

items.title: emission_flux
items.text:
emission_flux(*, saturate: bool = True) -> DataArray

Return the spatial emission in photons per second (after emission filters).

This is the ground truth data multiplied by the filtered emission rates, prior to convolution with the PSF.

This multiplies the per-fluorophore emission rates by the ground truth data to get the total emission flux for each voxel in the ground truth. The return array has dimensions (C, F, Z, Y, X). The units are photons/s.

Note, this integrates over all wavelengths. For finer control over the emission spectrum, you may wish to directly combine filtered_emission_rates with the ground truth data as needed.

This function is NOT used by run(). It is provided as a convenience for debugging and analysis. See also optical_image_per_fluor, which is similar to this function, but returns the image after convolution with the PSF. That function may return a different result than simply convolving this function's output with a single PSF, as it more accurately models multi-wavelength emission spectra (as superposition of multiple PSFs).

items.title: optical_image_per_fluor
items.text:
optical_image_per_fluor() -> DataArray

Return the optical image for each channel/fluorophore combination.

This is the emission from each fluorophore in each channel, after filtering by the optical configuration and convolution with the PSF.

The return array has dimensions (C, F, Z, Y, X). The units are photons/s.

items.title: optical_image
items.text:
optical_image() -> DataArray

Return the optical image as delivered to the detector.

This is the same as optical_image_per_fluor, but sums the contributions of all fluorophores in each channel (which a detector would not know). The return array has dimensions (C, Z, Y, X). The units are photons/s.

items.text:
Electron-multiplying CCD (EMCCD).

A CCD with an extra serial register of em_stages cells, clocked at high voltage. At each cell, every electron has a small chance (~1-2%) of creating a second electron by impact ionization, for a mean total gain em_gain = (1 + p) ** em_stages. This lifts the signal far above read noise, so single photons become visible. The cost is gain noise: the number of electrons out of the register varies widely for the same number in, with an excess noise factor that approaches 2 at high gain. An EMCCD therefore has the signal-to-noise ratio of an ideal detector with half its QE.

relative_gain/electrons_per_adu set the separate analog gain of the readout amplifier. relative_gain is relative to the pixel full_well, so at high EM gain electrons_per_adu is usually more convenient.

Excess noise factor of the EM register, which rises from 1 toward 2.

F = 2 (G - 1) G**(-(N + 1) / N) + 1 / G, for mean gain G over N stages (Robbins & Hadwen 2003, IEEE Trans. Electron Devices 50:1227). This follows from treating each stage as independent: an electron makes one extra electron with probability p = G**(1/N) - 1. items.title: PMT
items.text:
Photomultiplier tube, read out in analog (current-integrating) mode.

A photon hitting the photocathode releases a photoelectron (with probability qe). The photoelectron is accelerated onto a chain of 8-12 dynodes, each of which releases ~3-6 secondary electrons per incoming electron, for a total gain of 1e4-1e7 electrons per photoelectron at the anode. The anode current is integrated over the pixel dwell time, amplified, and digitized.

The gain is set by the high voltage (HV) across the tube, which is what microscope software calls the PMT "gain", "HV", or "master gain". Each dynode multiplies by delta ~ V**k (k = 0.7-0.8), so the total gain follows a power law (Hamamatsu PMT Handbook v4, Eq. 4-9):

gain = ref_gain * (hv / ref_hv) ** hv_exponent

hv is in whatever units ref_hv is. The presets describe Hamamatsu photosensor modules (as used in many confocals), whose HV is set by a 0.5-0.9 V control voltage. For a bare tube, use volts (e.g. ref_hv=1000). Experts can set hv_gain directly instead.

Each dynode's yield is random, which adds gain noise. With n equal stages of mean yield d = gain ** (1/n), the excess noise factor is F = 1 + 1/d + 1/d**2 + ... + 1/d**n, about d / (d - 1) (Handbook Eq. 4-25). Most of it comes from the first dynode, where the fewest electrons are involved. F is ~1.3 at a gain of 5e5, and rises as the HV is lowered (1.5 at 2e4). Real modules often run the first dynode at a higher voltage, which lowers F a bit; that is not modeled.

The amplifier adds a noise current, so the noise charge integrated over a pixel grows as sqrt(dwell), while the signal grows as dwell. It is negligible unless the HV (and so the gain) is low.

The anode current cannot rise without limit. With continuous light the limit comes from the voltage divider that sets the dynode voltages: anode current is drawn from it, the last dynodes lose voltage, and the gain drops (Handbook 5.1.3). Modules with an active divider stay linear almost up to their rated maximum average output current, then drop sharply (Hamamatsu H10720 datasheet, Fig. 8). Capacitors across the last dynodes supply short bursts of current, so the divider responds to the anode current averaged over its RC time constant (divider_time_constant_ms), not to single pixels: a lone bright pixel is fine, but a bright region dims itself and the scan lines after it. This is modeled as a gain factor 1 / (1 + (I_avg / I_max) ** 6) ** (1/6), where I_avg is a running average of the anode current in scan order (rows left to right, top to bottom, ignoring flyback): ~1% low at 0.6 I_max, 11% low at I_max. Lowering the HV raises the light level at which this happens.

The amplifier also has a finite bandwidth, so the signal from a bright pixel decays over the next few pixels along the scan line (time_constant_us, a first-order low-pass with f_c = 1 / (2 pi R C), Handbook Eq. 5-7). The filtered current is integrated over each pixel: with dwell T and time constant tau, a pixel keeps 1 - (tau/T)(1 - exp(-T/tau)) of its own charge (37% when tau = T), and the rest decays into the following pixels. This is the one-sided streak seen at short dwell times. The fast scan axis is the last (X) axis, scanned left to right, and each line starts dark (beam blanked during flyback). Off by default, since it makes pixels depend on their neighbors.

Known omissions:

  • The divider's response is a single time constant, and starts each image from the image's mean current (as when scanning repeatedly), ignoring any recovery during frame flyback.
  • A few % rise in gain before saturation ("over-linearity", Handbook Fig. 5-5).
  • Space charge saturation, which limits peak current (mA) and matters only for pulsed excitation, which microsim does not model.
  • Afterpulses (ion feedback a few hundred ns to µs after a photoelectron): a few % of extra delayed signal, with no published rates.
  • Temperature dependence, drift, and hysteresis of the gain (~1%).
  • Bidirectional scanning (which flips the streak on alternate lines).

items.title: HyD
items.text:
Hybrid photodetector (e.g. Leica HyD), read out by photon counting.

A photocathode (as in a PMT) releases a photoelectron, which is accelerated by ~8 kV straight into an avalanche diode. The impact alone creates ~1500 electron-hole pairs, and the avalanche multiplies them ~100x more. Because the first stage is so large, every photon gives nearly the same pulse (~3% spread), so pulses are counted rather than integrated. The output is a photon count: no gain noise (F = 1), and no read noise.

Each pulse briefly blinds the detector (dead_time_ns), so at high count rates some photons are missed: a true rate n is recorded as n / (1 + n * tau). At 40 Mcps and 1.5 ns, that loses ~6%. The dead time also spaces counts more regularly than random arrivals, so a mean count m has variance m / (1 + n * tau)**2 rather than m.

In Leica's "Standard" mode the count is multiplied by a gain; that is electrons_per_adu = 1 / gain here. The linearization Leica applies in that mode is not published, and is not modeled.

items.title: Confocal
items.text:
Point-scanning confocal.

The PSF is the probability that a photon emitted by a fluorophore at a given position (relative to the scan spot) passes the pinhole, times the relative excitation intensity there. The channel's power (OpticalConfig.power, in W/cm^2) is therefore interpreted as the peak irradiance at the focus, and exposure_ms as the per-pixel integration (dwell) time (it is not divided by the number of pixels). The excitation spot is computed at the excitation wavelengths, and excitation saturation is applied locally (it is strongest at the center of the spot).

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default pinhole_au float

Pinhole diameter in Airy units (1 AU = 1.22 * wavelength / NA, at the wavelength set by airy_unit_wavelength_nm).

1 type Literal['confocal'] 'confocal' airy_unit_wavelength_nm float | None

Wavelength (nm) at which pinhole_au is defined. By default, 1 AU is matched to the average emission filter band center of the channels sharing the pinhole (or, if not shared_pinhole, to each channel's band center).

None shared_pinhole bool

If True (the default), channels acquired together (in the same track, see Simulation.tracks) are detected through the same pinhole, as on many point scanners; the pinhole is set anew for each track. If False, each channel has its own pinhole, matched to its emission band.

True

items.title: Identity
items.text:
Optical modality in which PSF is not applied.

The idea is to use this modality when the ground truth fluorophore distribution is generated from a light microscope image, i.e., the PSF convolution is already applied on the image. This is useful primarily when you are more interested in the spectral properties (fluorophores, filters, bleedthrough, etc.) than the spatial properties (PSF, modality, etc.) in the simulation.

    fluorophore: Fluorophore, *, saturate: bool = True

Return the emission rate of a fluorophore with this configuration.

The emission rate is the total number of photons emitted per second per fluorophore, as a function of wavelength, prior to any filtering in the emission path. It's a vector with a single axis W, and singleton dimensions F and C. If saturate is True, excitation saturation is applied.

items.title: detected_fraction
items.text:
detected_fraction(
    fluorophore: Fluorophore,
    detector_qe: float | Spectrum | None = None,
) -> DataArray

Return the fraction of absorbed photons that are detected in this channel.

This is the number of photons detected per photon absorbed by fluorophore, as a function of emission wavelength: the quantum yield, times the emission spectrum (normalized to an area of 1), times the transmission of the emission filters and the detector QE. It does not include the fraction of emitted light collected by the objective (see ObjectiveLens.collection_efficiency).

items.title: filtered_emission_rate
items.text:
filtered_emission_rate(
    fluorophore: Fluorophore,
    detector_qe: float | Spectrum | None = None,
    *,
    saturate: bool = True,
) -> DataArray

Return the emission rate of a fluorophore with this config, after filters.

The emission rate is the number of photons emitted per second per fluorophore, as a function of wavelength, after being excited by this optical config, then passing through the emission path of this config. It's a vector with a single axis W, and singleton dimensions F and C.

This is the complete picture of the treatment of a specific fluorophore with this optical configuration. It takes into account:

- the excitation spectrum and extinction coefficient of the fluorophore
- the excitation filter/beamsplitter and light source spectra
- the quantum yield and emission spectrum of the fluorophore
- excitation saturation (unless `saturate` is False)
- the emission filter/beamsplitter spectra
- detector QE: `detector_qe`, or else this config's detector's QE

It does not include the fraction of emitted light collected by the objective (see Simulation.filtered_emission_rates, which does).

items.title: emission_band_center
items.text:
emission_band_center() -> float | None

Center wavelength of the emission filter passband.

This is the midpoint of the band where transmission is above half its peak (as in filter names, e.g. 525/50), combining all filters in the emission path. If they pass several bands, the one transmitting the most light is used, and transmission beyond 900 nm (e.g. near-infrared leaks) is ignored. Returns None if there are no emission filters, or if the band is open-ended: e.g. a longpass filter, still transmitting at the end of its spectrum. (A spectrum that only covers a narrow passband is fine: beyond its data, transmission is 0.)

items.title: First simulation
items.text: This page builds a simulation, runs it, and looks at the result of each stage. It needs the view extra for plotting (included in microsim[all]).

items.title: Build and run it
items.text:
from microsim import schema as ms
from microsim.util import ortho_plot

sim = ms.Simulation(
    truth_space=ms.ShapeScaleSpace(  # (1)!
        shape=(128, 512, 512),
        scale=(0.02, 0.01, 0.01),
    ),
    output_space={"downscale": 8},  # (2)!
    sample=ms.Sample(  # (3)!
        labels=[ms.MatsLines(density=0.5, length=30, azimuth=5)]
    ),
    detector=ms.CameraCMOS(),  # (4)!
)

result = sim.run()  # (5)!
ortho_plot(result)
  1. The truth space is the grid on which the sample is drawn and the optics are computed: 128 × 512 × 512 voxels (Z, Y, X), each 20 × 10 × 10 nm. That is a 2.56 × 5.12 × 5.12 µm volume. Lengths are in micrometers.
  2. The output space is the pixel grid of the final image. downscale: 8 bins the truth space by 8 along each axis, giving 16 × 64 × 64 pixels of 160 × 80 × 80 nm.
  3. The sample is a list of labels. MatsLines draws randomly oriented line segments, one voxel wide, with one fluorophore per voxel.
  4. The detector converts photons to gray values and adds noise. This is a CMOS camera with default settings.
  5. run() executes every stage and returns the digital image.

Everything not given has a default value. In this case:

Parameter Default modality Widefield() objective_lens 1.4 NA oil immersion (ObjectiveLens()) channels one FITC/GFP filter set, with 1 W/cm² of white light through the excitation filter fluorophore a placeholder fluorophore with flat spectra (see Samples) exposure_ms 100 ms settings NumPy backend (or CuPy if installed), float32, and a new random seed each time the Simulation is created

Dictionaries work too

As usual with pydantic models, any parameter can be given as a dictionary (or loaded from JSON) instead of an object. These are equivalent:

output_space = ms.DownscaledSpace(downscale=8)
output_space = {"downscale": 8}

When a field accepts several types, a "type" key selects one, as in {"type": "confocal", "pinhole_au": 1}. Unknown keys raise an error rather than being ignored.

items.title: Look at each stage
items.text:
run() computes four stages in order and returns the last one. Each stage also has its own method, and each returns an xarray.DataArray with named dimensions and physical coordinates (µm):

Method Dimensions Units ground_truth() (f, z, y, x) fluorophores per voxel filtered_emission_rates() (c, f, w) photons/s per fluorophore optical_image() (c, z, y, x) photons/s per voxel digital_image() (c, z, y, x) gray values

Dimension names: f fluorophore, c channel, w wavelength (nm), and z, y, x in µm.

truth = sim.ground_truth()  # the sample
optical = sim.optical_image()  # the light reaching the detector
digital = sim.digital_image(optical)  # (1)!
  1. Passing optical in avoids computing it again. This is useful to try several detectors or exposure times on one optical image.

Left to right: the ground truth (maximum projection), one plane of the optical image in the truth space, and one plane of the digital image in the output space.

The optical image is blurred but noise-free. The digital image is pixelated and noisy, and it is dim: the brightest pixel is about 10 gray values above the camera offset of 100.

items.title: Make it brighter
items.text:
The simulation works in physical units, so brightness follows from labeling density, illumination intensity, and exposure time, as on a real microscope. Here the sample is sparse (a single fluorophore per 10 nm voxel along each line) and the illumination is weak. Raising the irradiance of the channel to 10 W/cm² gives ten times as many photons:

from microsim.schema.optical_config import lib

sim.channels = [lib.FITC.model_copy(update={"power": 10})]  # (1)!
result = sim.run()
  1. lib.FITC is the default channel. model_copy makes a modified copy; setting lib.FITC.power directly would change it for every simulation in the session. power is in W/cm² at the sample.

A confocal microscope focuses a laser to a diffraction-limited spot and scans it, so its irradiance is far higher (kW/cm² to MW/cm² at the focus) and the time per pixel is far shorter (microseconds). For point-scanning modalities power is the peak irradiance at the focus and exposure_ms is the pixel dwell time. lib has laser lines for this:

sim.modality = ms.Confocal(pinhole_au=0.5)
sim.channels = [lib.LASER_488.model_copy(update={"power": 50_000})]  # W/cm² at focus
sim.exposure_ms = 0.01  # 10 µs per pixel
result = sim.run()

The digital image at the default 1 W/cm², at 10 W/cm², and as a confocal image with a 0.5 AU pinhole. Each panel is scaled to its own range.

items.title: Reproducibility
items.text:
The random lines in the sample and the noise come from a random number generator. To get the same result every time, set a seed:

sim = ms.Simulation(..., settings=ms.Settings(random_seed=42))

Without it, each new Simulation picks a random seed.

items.title: From PyPI
items.text:
pip install "microsim[all]"

Pin a specific version

microsim changes quickly, and releases can break the API or change simulation results for the same parameters. For any project you want to reproduce later, pin the exact version:

pip install "microsim[all]==0.x.y"

You can check the installed version with microsim.__version__.

The [all] extra installs the plotting, file I/O, and data-download dependencies used throughout these docs. The base package (pip install microsim) can run every simulation, but cannot plot results, write TIFF files, or fetch ground truth from OpenOrganelle.

items.title: GPU acceleration
items.text:
Most of the computation time goes into PSF generation and convolution. These can run on a GPU through CuPy or JAX. Neither is installed by default; follow their installation instructions for your GPU and CUDA version, then select the backend:

sim = ms.Simulation(..., settings=ms.Settings(np_backend="cupy"))

See Settings for details. A torch backend also exists, but is incomplete.

git clone https://github.com/tlambert03/microsim
cd microsim
uv sync

To build these docs locally:

uv run --group docs zensical serve

items.title: Overview
items.text: A microsim simulation follows the light from the sample to the detector. This page describes the parts of a simulation and the order in which they are used. The following pages cover each part in detail.

items.title: The Simulation object
items.text:
All parameters live on one Simulation object. Its fields map onto parts of a real experiment:

Field What it describes Guide truth_space the grid on which the sample and optics are computed Spaces output_space the pixel grid of the final image Spaces sample where the fluorophores are, and which fluorophores they are Samples channels light sources and filters, one entry per channel Channels tracks which channels are acquired at the same time Channels objective_lens numerical aperture, refractive indices, coverslip Modalities modality how the image is formed: widefield, confocal, ... Modalities detector camera or point detector, and its noise Detectors exposure_ms camera exposure, or pixel dwell time for point scanners Detectors settings compute backend, precision, random seed, caching Settings output_path where to save the result Saving and loading

Only truth_space and sample are required.

items.title: The stages
items.text:
Simulation.run() computes four things in order. Each is also available as a method, so you can stop at any stage, inspect the intermediate result, or change a parameter and repeat only the later stages.

flowchart TB
    subgraph S1 ["<span class='ms-stage'>1</span> ground_truth()"]
      direction LR
      sp[truth_space] --> gt["fluorophores per voxel<br/><code>(f, z, y, x)</code>"]
      sa[sample] --> gt
    end
    subgraph S2 ["<span class='ms-stage'>2</span> filtered_emission_rates()"]
      direction LR
      fl[fluorophore spectra] --> em["photons/s per fluorophore<br/><code>(c, f, w)</code>"]
      ch["channels, tracks"] --> em
      ob1[objective NA, specimen RI] --> em
      dq[detector QE] --> em
    end
    subgraph S3 ["<span class='ms-stage'>3</span> optical_image()"]
      direction LR
      mo[modality + objective → PSF] --> oi["photons/s per voxel<br/><code>(c, z, y, x)</code>"]
    end
    subgraph S4 ["<span class='ms-stage'>4</span> digital_image()"]
      direction LR
      os[output_space] --> di["gray values<br/><code>(c, z, y, x)</code>"]
      de[detector + exposure] --> di
    end
    S1 --> S3
    S2 --> S3
    S3 --> S4

1 Ground truth. Each label in the sample is drawn into the truth space. The result counts fluorophores per voxel, with one layer per label (f). See Samples.

2 Emission rates. For every pair of fluorophore and channel, microsim computes how many photons per second one fluorophore emits and how many reach the detector, as a function of wavelength (w). This includes the light source, excitation and emission filters, the fluorophore's absorption and emission spectra, extinction coefficient and quantum yield, the fraction of light the objective collects, and the detector's quantum efficiency. It has no spatial dimensions. Because every fluorophore is computed in every channel, bleedthrough and cross-excitation follow automatically. Channels acquired at the same time (tracks) excite the sample together. See Channels and Photon budget.

3 Optical image. The ground truth of each fluorophore is multiplied by its emission rate and convolved with the microscope's point spread function (PSF), then the fluorophores are summed within each channel. The result is the noise-free light distribution at the detector, in photons per second, still on the truth-space grid. See Modalities.

4 Digital image. The optical image is binned to the output space, multiplied by the exposure time, and passed through the detector model, which adds shot noise, dark current, gain, read noise, and digitization. See Detectors.

Ground truth (left), optical image (center), and digital image (right) for endoplasmic reticulum labeled with EGFP (green) and mitochondria labeled with mCherry (magenta). The ground truth is from OpenOrganelle; see the two-color tutorial.

There are two more methods for analysis. optical_image_per_fluor() returns the optical image before fluorophores are summed, as (c, f, z, y, x), which shows how much of each channel comes from each fluorophore. emission_flux() returns the emitted photons per voxel before blurring.

To simulate many samples with the same optics, run_batch() runs the simulation once per sample and yields each digital image. PSFs and emission rates are computed once and reused. Each sample gets its own random seed, derived from settings.random_seed, and if output_path is set, result i is written to <stem>_<i>.<suffix>.

items.title: Units
items.text:
microsim uses one unit per kind of quantity:

Quantity Unit lengths (space scale, extent) µm wavelengths nm irradiance (power) W/cm² exposure and dwell time ms extinction coefficient M⁻¹ cm⁻¹ fluorescence lifetime ns

items.title: Outputs are labeled arrays
items.text:
Every stage returns an xarray.DataArray. Its dimensions have names, and z, y, x carry coordinates in µm, so you can select and reduce by name:

digital = sim.run()
digital.sel(c="FITC")  # select a channel by name
digital.isel(z=8).plot()  # plot a plane (needs matplotlib)
sim.ground_truth().max("z")  # maximum projection

Use digital.values (or numpy.asarray(digital)) for a plain NumPy array. With a GPU backend, digital.data is a GPU array; see Settings.

items.title: What is (and isn't) modeled
items.text:
microsim aims to make each modeled step physically correct, and to state the approximations. The guide pages list the details for each part. In summary, these are not modeled at present:

  • photobleaching, blinking, and other time-dependent fluorophore behavior (emission is a steady-state rate)
  • triplet and other dark states, and stimulated emission
  • scattering, absorption, and aberrations from the sample (other than the refractive index mismatch handled by the PSF model)
  • out-of-focus background other than what the PSF produces, and autofluorescence
  • pixel-to-pixel variation of sCMOS cameras
  • the camera's physical pixel size and magnification (the output pixel size is set by output_space)

items.title: Channels
items.text:
A channel is one optical configuration of the microscope: the light source and the filters it uses to excite the sample and to select the emitted light. Simulation.channels is a list of OpticalConfig objects, and the output has one image per channel along the c dimension.

The default is a single FITC (GFP) channel.

from microsim.schema.optical_config import lib

sim = ms.Simulation(..., channels=[lib.FITC, lib.TRITC])

A fluorophore's absorption and emission spectra (normalized to their peaks), the excitation light that reaches the sample, and the transmission of the emission path. The emission path combines every filter in it: the dichroic mirror reflects the excitation light toward the sample and transmits the emission to the detector. Shaded: the absorption spectrum weighted by the excitation light, and the emission that passes the emission path. Hover for values. The filter sets in this and the other charts of this guide are measured spectra from FPbase: Chroma's ET filter sets (below), and the Semrock filters of an example microscope.

items.title: Built-in filter sets
items.text:
microsim.schema.optical_config.lib has idealized versions of common filter sets, built from smooth bandpass and longpass edges, with the nominal band edges of Chroma's ET filter sets. They are not measured spectra, and are meant for quick simulations; for real filters, load them from FPbase (below). The interactive charts in this guide use the measured spectra of the Chroma sets.

Name Excitation Dichroic Emission Chroma set (FPbase) DAPI 350/50 400 LP 460/50 "PMtA2n::Chroma 49000" ECFP 436/20 455 LP 480/40 "PMtA2n::Chroma 49001" FITC 470/40 495 LP 525/50 "PMtA2n::Chroma 49002" EYFP 500/20 515 LP 535/30 "PMtA2n::Chroma 49003" TRITC 545/25 565 LP 605/70 "PMtA2n::Chroma 49004" DSRED 545/30 570 LP 620/60 "PMtA2n::Chroma 49005" CY5 620/60 660 LP 700/75 "PMtA2n::Chroma 49006" CY7 710/75 760 LP 810/90 "PMtA2n::Chroma 49007"

Bandpass filters are written as center/width in nm. The last column is the string that loads the measured set (Filter sets from FPbase).

For point-scanning confocals, lib also has laser lines: a laser, a dichroic, and an emission bandpass, with generic filter values. Their power is 1e5 W/cm², the peak irradiance at the focus (about 50 µW at the sample with a 1.4 NA objective).

Name Laser Dichroic Emission LASER_405 405 nm 420 LP 450/50 LASER_445 445 nm 455 LP 480/40 LASER_488 488 nm 495 LP 525/50 LASER_515 515 nm 520 LP 550/40 LASER_561 561 nm 570 LP 600/50 LASER_640 640 nm 650 LP 690/50

items.title: Filter sets from FPbase
items.text:
FPbase lets you enter the optical configurations of your own microscope, with measured spectra of its light sources, filters, and detectors, and has many microscopes entered by others. These configurations can be loaded in microsim with a string of the form "<microscope id>::<config name>":

sim = ms.Simulation(..., channels=["wKqWbg::Widefield Green"])
# equivalent:
ms.OpticalConfig.from_fpbase("wKqWbg", "Widefield Green")

The microscope ID is in the URL of its FPbase page, e.g. fpbase.org/microscope/wKqWbgApvguSNDSRZNSfpN/ (the first few characters are enough). Configuration names are not case-sensitive. Some FPbase microscopes with filter catalogs:

  • Chroma filter sets
  • Semrock filter sets
  • Nikon filter sets
  • Zeiss filter sets

items.title: Building your own
items.text:
ms.OpticalConfig(
    name="GFP, 488 laser",
    lights=[ms.LightSource.laser(488)],
    filters=[
        ms.Longpass(cuton=495, placement="BS"),
        ms.Bandpass(bandcenter=525, bandwidth=50, placement="EM"),
    ],
    power=2000,  # W/cm² at the sample
)

items.title: Filters
items.text:
Filter Parameters Bandpass bandcenter, bandwidth (nm), peak transmission Longpass cuton (nm), edge slope, transmission Shortpass cutoff (nm), edge slope, transmission SpectrumFilter a measured transmission Spectrum

placement says where a filter sits in the light path:

placement Excitation path Emission path Typical use "EX" transmission (not used) excitation filter "EM" (not used) transmission emission filter "BS" 1 − transmission transmission dichroic that reflects excitation "BSi" transmission 1 − transmission dichroic that reflects emission "ALL" transmission transmission e.g. a neutral density filter

The defaults are "EX" for Shortpass, "EM" for Longpass, and "ALL" for Bandpass and SpectrumFilter, so set placement explicitly for bandpass filters. Filters in the same path are multiplied together.

items.title: Light sources
items.text: lights is a list of LightSource objects, each with an emission spectrum. LightSource.laser(488) makes a narrow line at 488 nm. With no light source, the channel is illuminated by flat white light, so the excitation filters alone set the spectrum.

items.title: Illumination power
items.text:
OpticalConfig.power is the irradiance at the sample in W/cm², summed over all wavelengths after the excitation filters. If it is not set, the irradiance is 1 W/cm².

LightSource.power sets relative power only

When a channel has several light sources, each source's spectrum is multiplied by its power before they are added, so power sets their relative weight. For sources whose spectra have the same sum, such as LightSource.laser lines, that is each source's share of the total. The total is always OpticalConfig.power (or 1 W/cm²). Set power on the OpticalConfig to change brightness.

Rough orders of magnitude for the irradiance at the sample:

Microscope Irradiance widefield, arc lamp or LED 0.1–10 W/cm² widefield, laser 10–1000 W/cm² point-scanning confocal, at focus 10–1000 kW/cm²

For point-scanning modalities, power is the peak irradiance at the center of the focused spot. See Modalities. To change the power of a library channel, use e.g. lib.LASER_488.model_copy(update={"power": 1e4}).

items.title: Per-channel exposure
items.text:
OpticalConfig.exposure_ms overrides Simulation.exposure_ms for one channel:

channels = [
    lib.FITC.model_copy(update={"exposure_ms": 50}),
    lib.TRITC.model_copy(update={"exposure_ms": 200}),
]

Modifying the library configurations

The objects in lib are shared. Use model_copy(update={...}) to make a modified copy, rather than assigning to lib.FITC.power directly, which would change it everywhere in your session.

items.title: Bleedthrough and cross-excitation
items.text:
microsim computes every fluorophore in every channel, so crosstalk needs no extra setup. A fluorophore excited by another channel's light (cross-excitation), or whose emission passes another channel's filter (bleedthrough), appears in that channel in proportion to the overlap of the spectra. Which light sources are on while a channel is recorded depends on whether channels are acquired one after another or at the same time.

Detected photons per molecule for two fluorophores in two channels, acquired one after the other (each channel is excited only by its own light). Dashed cells are crosstalk: the fluorophore gives less than half of that channel's signal. tdTomato absorbs only weakly in the FITC excitation band, but it is bright, and a 500 nm longpass emitter (Chroma ET500lp, in place of the ET525/50m of the FITC set 49002) passes nearly all of its emission: per molecule, it gives about 77% as much signal in the green channel as EGFP. With the ET525/50m bandpass, its share drops to about 0.5%. Select FITC (Chroma 49002) as channel 1 to compare.

To see where the signal in each channel comes from in an image, use optical_image_per_fluor(), which keeps the fluorophore dimension:

sim = ms.Simulation(
    truth_space=ms.ShapeScaleSpace(shape=(64, 512, 512), scale=0.064),
    sample=[
        ms.FluorophoreDistribution(
            distribution=ms.CosemLabel(dataset="jrc_hela-3", label="er-mem_pred"),
            fluorophore="EGFP",
        ),
        ms.FluorophoreDistribution(
            distribution=ms.CosemLabel(dataset="jrc_hela-3", label="mito-mem_pred"),
            fluorophore="tdTomato",
        ),
    ],
    channels=[lib.FITC, fitc_longpass],  # (1)!
)
per_fluor = sim.optical_image_per_fluor()  # (c, f, z, y, x)
per_fluor.sum(["z", "y", "x"])  # total photons/s from each fluorophore in each channel
  1. fitc_longpass is lib.FITC with its emission filter replaced by ms.Longpass(cuton=500, placement="EM").

A HeLa cell with EGFP on the ER and tdTomato on the mitochondria, recorded in the green channel with a 525/50 bandpass (top) and a 500 nm longpass (bottom) emission filter. Each row has one display range, so each panel shows its true contribution. With the longpass filter, the mitochondria appear in the green channel.

items.title: Sequential and simultaneous acquisition
items.text:
By default, channels are acquired one after another, so each channel is excited only by its own light sources. Simulation.tracks groups channels that are acquired at the same time, as in the tracks of a point scanner. All light sources of all channels in a track are on together, and each channel's detector records at the same time, so a fluorophore can be excited by any light source of its track:

from microsim.schema.optical_config.lib import (
    LASER_405,
    LASER_488,
    LASER_561,
    LASER_640,
)

sim = ms.Simulation(
    ...,
    channels=[LASER_405, LASER_488, LASER_561, LASER_640],
    tracks=[[0, 2], [1, 3]],  # or by name: [["405", "561"], ["488", "640"]]
)
tracks Meaning "sequential" (default) each channel is its own track "simultaneous" one track with all channels a list of lists channels by index in channels, or by name

Each list is shorthand for a Track, e.g. Track(channels=[0, 2]), and every channel must be in exactly one track.

  • A light source listed in several channels of a track (e.g. two detection windows behind one laser) is one light source, on once, so those channels must have the same power and excitation-side filters (including the dichroic). Channels in a track must have either the same light sources or none in common.
  • On a point scanner, the channels of a track have one pixel dwell time, so they must have the same exposure_ms.
  • Each channel detects through its own filters, including its own dichroic. On a real scanner, the channels of a track share one (multiband) dichroic; give them matching dichroics if that matters for your simulation.
  • With a Confocal modality, the channels of a track are detected through one pinhole (unless shared_pinhole=False).

items.title: Plotting spectra
items.text:
These need the view extra. For one channel:

oc = ms.OpticalConfig.from_fpbase("wKqWbg", "Widefield Green")
oc.plot()  # all filter spectra


fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 3.2))
oc.plot_excitation(
    ax=axes[0]
)  # light source and excitation filters, and the photon flux
oc.plot_emission(ax=axes[1])  # emission filters, and their combined transmission

For a whole simulation, Simulation.plot() shows, for each channel (columns): the absorption cross sections, the excitation path, the absorption rates (with the emission spectra, dashed), the emission path, and the photons collected from each fluorophore. Here EGFP and mCherry in the FITC and TRITC channels:

sim.plot()

items.title: Spectral detection
items.text:
lib.spectral_detector returns a list of channels that split an emission range into equal bins, as on a spectral confocal:

channels = lib.spectral_detector(bins=8, min_wave=480, max_wave=600, lasers=[488, 561])

This is a simplified model: each bin is an ideal rectangular filter, and a dichroic reflects a 10 nm band around each laser line.

items.title: Detectors
items.text:
The detector turns the optical image (photons per second at each pixel) into the digital image (integer gray values). This is where the exposure time enters, and where most of the noise comes from.

sim = ms.Simulation(..., detector=ms.CameraCMOS(qe=0.8, read_noise=1.5))
Detector camera_type Models CameraCCD "CCD" CCD cameras CameraEMCCD "EMCCD" electron-multiplying CCD cameras CameraCMOS "CMOS" CMOS and sCMOS cameras PMT "PMT" photomultiplier tubes, analog readout HyD "HyD" hybrid photodetectors, photon counting

In dictionary form, camera_type selects the class: detector={"camera_type": "EMCCD", "em_gain": 300}.

Without a detector

If detector is None (the default), the digital image is the expected number of photons per pixel: the optical image times the exposure time, binned to the output space, with no noise of any kind. Add a detector to get shot noise.

A noise-free image (the ER of a HeLa cell, simulated by microsim) recorded by different cameras, all with QE = 1. The noise is drawn in your browser, with the same steps and distributions as microsim's detector model. At a few photons per pixel, the CCD's read noise dominates; the sCMOS is close to the shot-noise limit; the EMCCD's gain lifts single photons above its read noise, at the cost of extra gain noise.

items.title: Exposure time
items.text:
Simulation.exposure_ms is the integration time per pixel, in milliseconds:

  • for a camera, the exposure time of each frame;
  • for a point scanner, the pixel dwell time (typically 0.0005–0.01 ms).

A channel can override it with OpticalConfig.exposure_ms, and digital_image(exposure_ms=...) overrides both, which is a quick way to compare exposure times on one optical image:

optical = sim.optical_image()
short = sim.digital_image(optical, exposure_ms=10)
long = sim.digital_image(optical, exposure_ms=1000)

items.title: The detector simulation pipeline
items.text:
All detectors run the same sequence of steps. They differ in their parameters, and in which steps do nothing for them.

  1. Expected signal. Photons per second × integration time gives the mean number of photoelectrons per pixel. Dark current (and clock-induced charge, for cameras) is added.
  2. Shot noise. The number of photoelectrons is drawn from a Poisson distribution with that mean.
  3. Full well. A camera pixel cannot hold more than full_well electrons.
  4. Multiplication. EMCCDs and PMTs multiply each electron by a random gain before readout. The randomness adds noise.
  5. Readout. The amplifier adds Gaussian read noise, and the ADC converts electrons to gray values, rounded and clipped to the top of the bit_depth range. Then any digital gain and the offset are applied, and the result is clipped to the range again.

The parameters shared by all detectors:

Parameter Meaning qe quantum efficiency, 0–1: a number, or a Spectrum over wavelength dark_current thermally generated electrons (or dark counts) per pixel per second read_noise electrons rms, added once per frame offset gray value added to every pixel bit_depth output gray values are clipped to 0 … 2bit_depth − 1 averaging number of frames (or scan passes) averaged into each image electrons_per_adu electrons per gray value, as on a camera datasheet relative_gain analog gain relative to the setting at which full_well maps to the maximum gray value (cameras only)

Give either electrons_per_adu or relative_gain, not both. For cameras the default is relative_gain=1, which maps a full pixel to the top of the ADC range.

QE is applied in the optical image

The detector's qe is applied per wavelength when the emission rates are computed (Photon budget), not in the detector step. If you swap detectors on an existing optical image, the new detector's QE is not used. Recompute the optical image, or compare detectors with similar QE. See #152.

Noise in more detail

Shot noise. Photons arrive at random, so the count in a pixel is Poisson distributed: its variance equals its mean \(n\), and the best possible signal-to-noise ratio is \(\sqrt{n}\).

Read noise \(\sigma_r\) is added once per readout, independent of the signal, so the SNR of a camera without gain is

\[ \text{SNR} = \frac{n}{\sqrt{n + n_\text{dark} + \sigma_r^2}} \]

Read noise dominates when \(n \lesssim \sigma_r^2\).

Excess noise. A random gain \(g\) per electron multiplies the variance by the excess noise factor \(F = \langle g^2 \rangle / \langle g \rangle^2\). After the gain, read noise is negligible but

\[ \text{SNR} = \sqrt{\frac{n}{F}} \]

so gain noise acts like dividing the QE by \(F\). microsim draws the multiplied signal from a gamma distribution with the right mean and variance. This is exact for an EMCCD at high gain, and approximate (in the shape of the distribution, not its mean or variance) at low gain.

Quantization. Rounding to integer gray values adds a uniform error of variance 1/12 gray value². It matters when electrons_per_adu is large compared with the read noise.

Averaging. With averaging=N, the signal and dark current are integrated for N times the exposure, read noise is added N times, and the result is divided by N. Brightness is unchanged, and noise is reduced.

items.title: SNR against signal
items.text: SNR of each camera, relative to an ideal detector that adds only shot noise, from the formulas above. Read noise matters at low signal; the EMCCD's gain removes it, at the cost of the excess noise factor, which caps its relative SNR at \(1/\sqrt{F} \approx 71\%\).

items.title: CCD
items.text: CameraCCD: all pixels share one output amplifier. Typical values: QE 0.5–0.7, read noise 5–10 e⁻, full well 15,000–20,000 e⁻.

items.title: EMCCD
items.text:
CameraEMCCD adds an electron-multiplying register before the amplifier. Each of its em_stages cells (604 by default) multiplies the charge by a small random amount, for a mean gain em_gain (typically 100–1000). The signal is lifted far above the read noise, so single photons become detectable, but the excess noise factor rises toward 2: at high gain an EMCCD has the SNR of a noise-free detector with half its QE.

Excess noise factor of the EM register, CameraEMCCD.excess_noise_factor.

ms.CameraEMCCD(qe=0.95, em_gain=300, read_noise=50, electrons_per_adu=20)

With an EMCCD, electrons_per_adu is usually easier to reason about than relative_gain, because relative_gain refers to the pixel full well, before the EM gain.

items.title: CMOS and sCMOS
items.text:
CameraCMOS: each pixel has its own amplifier. Typical values for a scientific CMOS: QE 0.7–0.95, read noise 1–2 e⁻, electrons_per_adu around 0.5 at 16 bits.

sCMOS pixel-to-pixel variation is not modeled

The model applies the same gain, offset, and read noise to every pixel. Real sCMOS sensors vary from pixel to pixel, and some pixels are much noisier than average, so simulated sCMOS images are more uniform than real ones. Per-pixel gain, offset, and read noise maps are on the roadmap.

Default camera settings

All cameras default to QE 1, read noise 6 e⁻, full well 18,000 e⁻, 12 bits, offset 100, and dark current 0.001 e⁻/pixel/s. These are not meant to match any particular camera. Set the values from your camera's datasheet, or start from the library model lib.ICX285.

items.title: Point detectors
items.text:
A point scanner records one pixel at a time, so its detectors have no pixels to hold charge, no full well, and no relative_gain. Set their gain with electrons_per_adu, or the parameters below. exposure_ms is the pixel dwell time.

The same confocal optical image, recorded with 1 µs pixel dwell by a GaAsP PMT at two control voltages and by a HyD in photon-counting mode, without and with 4× averaging. At 0.9 V many PMT pixels clip at the top of the 12-bit range. The HyD gives raw photon counts. From the point-scanning detectors tutorial.

items.title: PMT
items.text:
PMT models a photomultiplier tube read out in analog mode. A photoelectron from the photocathode is multiplied by a chain of dynodes, and the resulting current is integrated over the dwell time.

  • Gain. Set the high voltage hv as on the microscope. The gain follows a power law, ref_gain × (hv / ref_hv) ** hv_exponent. The defaults model a Hamamatsu GaAsP photosensor module controlled by a 0.5–0.9 V signal, with a gain of 5 × 10⁵ at 0.8 V. To set the gain directly, use hv_gain instead.
  • Gain noise. The excess noise factor follows from the gain per dynode, and increases as the HV is lowered (about 1.3 at 0.9 V, 1.5 at 0.5 V for the default tube).
  • Digital gain. digital_gain multiplies the digitized signal, like the digital gain setting in some acquisition software. It amplifies signal and noise equally.
  • Saturation. If max_output_current_ua is set, the gain drops as the average anode current approaches that limit. The current is averaged over divider_time_constant_ms along the scan, so a bright region dims itself and the lines that follow it.
  • Amplifier bandwidth. If time_constant_us > 0, the signal of each pixel leaks into the next few pixels along X, producing a streak at short dwell times.

Gain and excess noise factor of the PMT presets in detectors.lib across their control voltage range.

items.title: HyD
items.text:
HyD models a hybrid photodetector (as in Leica HyD detectors) in photon-counting mode. Every photon gives nearly the same pulse, so pulses are counted: no gain noise and no read noise. With the default electrons_per_adu=1, the output is the photon count.

After each pulse the detector is blind for dead_time_ns (1.5 ns by default), so at high count rates some photons are missed: a true rate \(n\) is recorded as \(n / (1 + n\tau)\), about 6% low at 40 million counts per second. Dead time also makes the counts more regular than Poisson.

Fraction of photons counted by a photon counter with a non-paralyzable dead time, against the true photon rate.

items.title: Detector library
items.text:
microsim.schema.detectors.lib has detectors with published or measured parameters:

Name Type Notes ICX285 CCD Sony ICX285 sensor, with its QE spectrum PMT_GAASP PMT GaAsP photocathode, QE spectrum from FPbase, 2 µA max. output PMT_MULTIALKALI PMT multialkali photocathode, QE 0.2, 100 µA max. output HYD_SP8 HyD GaAsP hybrid detector POWER_HYD_R HyD red-extended GaAsP hybrid detector

The source code of detectors/lib.py lists where each value comes from.

The detector docstrings in the API reference describe each model in more detail, including what is not modeled.

items.title: Modalities and the PSF
items.text:
The modality decides how the optical image is formed from the ground truth. For the modalities available now, that means choosing a point spread function (PSF) and convolving each fluorophore's emission with it.

sim = ms.Simulation(..., modality=ms.Confocal(pinhole_au=1))
Modality PSF Image formed by Widefield (default) emission PSF camera Confocal excitation PSF × (emission PSF ⊗ pinhole) point scanning Identity none (ground truth is already an image)

The optical image of the same random lines in widefield and in confocal with a 1 AU pinhole (XY plane through the middle of the volume, and an XZ section). This is the noise-free optical image, in the truth space: before binning to the output pixels, and before the detector. The confocal removes most of the out-of-focus light.

items.title: Widefield
items.text: The whole field is illuminated uniformly and imaged onto a camera. Each fluorophore's emission is convolved with the emission PSF. Every plane of the PSF sums to about 1: a defocused point source spreads its light over more pixels, but the total light recorded from it is the same at any focus.

items.title: Confocal
items.text:
A focused laser spot is scanned across the sample, and the emission passes a pinhole before reaching a point detector. The confocal PSF is the product of

  • the excitation PSF: the relative irradiance of the focused spot, 1 at the center, and
  • the effective detection PSF: the emission PSF convolved with the pinhole, which is the fraction of collected light that passes the pinhole for an emitter at each position.
\[ \text{PSF}_\text{confocal}(x, y, z) = \text{PSF}_\text{ex}(x, y, z) \cdot \big[\text{PSF}_\text{em}(\cdot, \cdot, z) \ast P\big](x, y) \]

where \(P\) is the pinhole, a disk of diameter pinhole_au, and \(\ast\) is a 2D convolution in each plane. \(\text{PSF}_\text{ex}\) is 1 at the focus, and \(\text{PSF}_\text{em}\) sums to 1 in each plane, so the confocal PSF at the focus is the fraction of the collected light that passes the pinhole.

pinhole_au is the pinhole diameter in Airy units, where 1 AU is 1.22 λ / NA, measured in the sample. Smaller pinholes reject more out-of-focus light and slightly improve resolution, at the cost of signal.

The pinhole has one physical size for all the light that passes it, so λ is one wavelength per pinhole, not the wavelength of each fluorophore:

  • By default, λ is the center of the channel's emission filter passband (e.g. 525 nm for a 525/50 filter). As on many point scanners, the channels of a track are detected through one pinhole, and λ is the average of their band centers. With shared_pinhole=False, each channel has its own pinhole, matched to its own band.
  • If a channel sharing the pinhole has no band-limited emission filter (e.g. only a longpass), λ is the mean wavelength of the emission detected in all the channels sharing it, and microsim warns.
  • airy_unit_wavelength_nm sets λ directly.

The excitation spot is computed at the excitation wavelengths. With several lasers, or a broadband source, the light each fluorophore absorbs is grouped into bands at most excitation_bin_width_nm wide (Settings), and the spot is the sum of the spots at each band's wavelength, weighted by the light absorbed in it.

For a point-scanning modality:

  • power on the channel is the peak irradiance at the center of the spot (often kW/cm² or more), not an average over the field.
  • exposure_ms is the pixel dwell time (often 0.0005–0.01 ms), and is not divided among pixels. Channels acquired together (in one track) must have the same dwell time.
  • Saturation is applied at each position of the excitation spot rather than to the emission rate.
  • Downsampling to the output space averages rather than sums (Spaces).
  • Point-scanning microscopes record with a point detector (PMT or HyD), but microsim accepts any detector.

Widefield and confocal PSFs computed by microsim at 1.4 NA, 525 nm emission and 488 nm excitation, each scaled to its own peak. With show the signal lost at the pinhole, the confocal PSF is instead scaled by the fraction of the collected light that passes the pinhole, so it dims as the pinhole closes. Signal from a thin plane: the light recorded from a thin, uniform fluorescent layer at each distance from the focus. In widefield it is the same at every depth, so out-of-focus planes contribute as much as the focal plane; the pinhole removes it, more so the smaller it is. Smaller pinholes also narrow the PSF, mostly below 1 AU, while passing less light.

items.title: Identity
items.text: Identity applies no PSF. Use it when the ground truth is already a microscope image (for example, a real widefield image) and you are interested in the spectral and detector parts of the simulation: fluorophores, filters, bleedthrough, and noise: modality=ms.Identity(), or {"type": "identity"}.

items.title: Objective lens
items.text:
ObjectiveLens sets the numerical aperture and the refractive indices used by the PSF model. The default is a 1.4 NA oil immersion objective.

ms.Simulation(
    ...,
    objective_lens=ms.ObjectiveLens(
        numerical_aperture=1.2,
        immersion_medium_ri=1.333,
        immersion_medium_ri_spec=1.333,
        specimen_ri=1.333,
    ),
)
Parameter Default Meaning numerical_aperture 1.4 NA; cannot exceed the immersion refractive index immersion_medium_ri 1.515 refractive index of the immersion medium specimen_ri 1.47 refractive index of the sample coverslip_ri 1.515 refractive index of the coverslip coverslip_thickness_um 170 coverslip thickness *_spec versions same the values the objective was designed for working_distance_um 150 design working distance

The *_spec parameters describe the conditions the objective is corrected for. When the actual values differ (a coverslip of the wrong thickness, or the wrong immersion oil), the PSF shows the resulting spherical aberration.

The NA also sets the collection efficiency (the fraction of emitted light that enters the objective), so a lower NA gives a dimmer image as well as a larger PSF.

The PSF model

PSFs are computed with a vectorial model of a high-NA objective that includes the Gibson–Lanni optical path difference for mismatched coverslip, immersion, and specimen refractive indices (microsim.psf).

The same PSF is used for the whole volume (it is spatially invariant), and is computed for a point source at the coverslip surface. Aberrations that grow with imaging depth into a mismatched specimen are therefore not included.

items.title: Emission spectrum and the PSF
items.text:
The PSF depends on wavelength, and a fluorophore emits over a range of wavelengths. By default, microsim computes one PSF per fluorophore and channel, at the centroid wavelength of the detected emission. For a more accurate result, it can split the detected emission into several wavelength bins and sum one PSF per bin, weighted by the photons in that bin:

ms.Settings(spectral_bins_per_emission_channel=3)

This takes proportionally longer. See Settings.

items.title: PSF caching
items.text: PSFs are cached in memory and on disk, keyed by every parameter that affects them, so repeating a simulation with a different sample, or with a detector with the same QE, does not recompute them. (The QE changes the spectrum of the detected light, and so the wavelengths at which the PSFs are computed.) See Settings.

items.title: Photon budget
items.text:
This page explains how microsim calculates the number of photons a fluorophore emits and how many of them reach the detector. These calculations happen in filtered_emission_rates(), before anything spatial is computed.

The photon budget of one molecule, calculated as microsim does. Excitation: the light at the sample times the absorption cross section gives the absorption rate. Emission: the absorption rate times the quantum yield (and saturation, if any) is spread over the emission spectrum, then multiplied by the emission path, the detector QE, and the fraction of light the objective collects (1.4 NA and specimen refractive index 1.47, the ObjectiveLens defaults). The light, cross section, and emission are drawn relative to their peaks, so each shaded area is the product of the curves in its plot (times the collection efficiency, for the detected light). Hover for values. The filter sets are measured spectra from FPbase (Channels). With the starting values (EGFP, Chroma's FITC set 49002, 1 W/cm², no detector QE), one molecule absorbs about 390 photons/s and gives about 53 detected photons/s, or about 5 in a 100 ms exposure. Typical widefield irradiance is 0.1–10 W/cm²; the peak irradiance of a confocal spot is 10–1000 kW/cm² (Channels). Fluorophores without a known lifetime do not saturate.

items.title: In short
items.text:
For each fluorophore in each channel:

  1. The light source and excitation filters give a photon flux at the sample.
  2. The fluorophore's absorption cross section turns that into an absorption rate.
  3. The quantum yield and emission spectrum turn that into an emission rate, per wavelength.
  4. The emission filters, the detector's QE, and the fraction of light the objective collects reduce it to the detected rate.

Steps 1 and 2 are the Excitation plot of the chart above, and steps 3 and 4 the Emission plot.

The result is an array with dimensions (c, f, w): photons per second, per fluorophore, for every channel, fluorophore, and wavelength. Keeping the wavelength lets the next stage use a PSF for the actual emission color. Keeping every channel–fluorophore pair is what produces bleedthrough.

These rates are for a fluorophore at the channel's power: anywhere in a widefield field of view, or at the center of the focused spot in a confocal. By default they include excitation saturation at that irradiance.

You can compute each step on its own:

oc, fluor = lib.FITC, ms.Fluorophore.from_fpbase("EGFP")

oc.illumination_flux_density  # photons/cm²/s, per wavelength
fluor.absorption_cross_section  # cm², per wavelength
oc.absorption_rate(fluor)  # photons/s absorbed
oc.total_emission_rate(fluor)  # photons/s emitted
oc.filtered_emission_rate(fluor)  # photons/s through the emission path
sim.filtered_emission_rates()  # all pairs, with QE and collection efficiency
sim.filtered_emission_rates(saturate=False)  # the same, without saturation

The OpticalConfig methods describe a channel on its own. Simulation also accounts for channels that are acquired at the same time.

items.title: The details
items.text:
1. Absorption cross section

The excitation spectrum from FPbase (or your Fluorophore) is normalized to 1 at its peak and multiplied by the extinction coefficient \(\varepsilon\) to give \(\varepsilon(\lambda)\) in M⁻¹ cm⁻¹. The absorption cross section of one molecule, in cm², is

\[ \sigma(\lambda) = \frac{\ln(10) \cdot 10^3 \cdot \varepsilon(\lambda)}{N_A} \]

where \(N_A\) is Avogadro's number. For EGFP (\(\varepsilon = 55{,}900\) M⁻¹ cm⁻¹) the peak cross section is about \(2.1 \times 10^{-16}\) cm².

2. Illumination

The illumination spectrum is the light source spectrum (the sum of the light sources, weighted by their relative power), multiplied by the transmission of every filter in the excitation path at the light source's wavelengths, so a laser stays a single line. With no light source, it is flat white light through the excitation filters. It is scaled so that its sum over wavelength equals the channel's power, \(P\) (1 W/cm² if not set). This gives the irradiance \(E(\lambda)\) in W/cm² per wavelength bin, which is converted to a photon flux density, in photons/cm²/s:

\[ \Phi(\lambda) = \frac{E(\lambda) \, \lambda}{h c} \] 3. Absorption rate

The rate at which one molecule absorbs photons is the overlap of the cross section and the photon flux, summed over the wavelengths of the illumination (the cross section is interpolated there):

\[ k = \sum_\lambda \sigma(\lambda) \, \Phi(\lambda) \] 4. Emission rate

The emission spectrum \(I_\text{em}(\lambda)\) is normalized to unit sum, and scaled by the quantum yield \(\phi\) and the absorption rate:

\[ R_\text{em}(\lambda) = \phi \, k \, \frac{I_\text{em}(\lambda)}{\sum_{\lambda'} I_\text{em}(\lambda')} \]

(With saturation, \(k\) is replaced by \(k / (1 + k\tau)\).)

5. Emission path and detector

The emitted light is multiplied by the combined transmission \(T_\text{em}(\lambda)\) of every filter in the emission path, and by the detector's quantum efficiency \(\text{QE}(\lambda)\), if a detector is set, both interpolated at the wavelengths of the emission spectrum:

\[ R_\text{det}(\lambda) = R_\text{em}(\lambda) \, T_\text{em}(\lambda) \, \text{QE}(\lambda) \]

QE is applied here, per wavelength, rather than in the detector model. The optical image therefore depends on the detector, so if you change to a detector with a different QE, compute the optical image again. (#152 tracks this.)

6. Collection efficiency

A fluorophore emits in all directions, and the objective collects only the light within its acceptance cone. The fraction collected is the solid angle of the cone divided by that of a sphere:

\[ \eta = \frac{1 - \cos\theta}{2}, \qquad \sin\theta = \min\left(\frac{\text{NA}}{n_s}, 1\right) \]

where \(n_s\) is the refractive index of the specimen. The angle is measured in the specimen, where the light is emitted. For a 1.4 NA objective and \(n_s = 1.47\), \(\eta = 0.35\); for a 0.8 NA objective and \(n_s = 1.33\), 0.10.

This ignores reflection losses at interfaces, the dipole emission pattern, supercritical-angle fluorescence near the coverslip, and the transmission of the objective and other optics.

items.title: Channels acquired together
items.text:
When channels are acquired at the same time (in one track), all of their light sources are on, so a fluorophore absorbs from all of them. Its absorption rate is then the sum over the light sources of the track, each at its own channel's power:

\[ k = \sum_\text{sources} \sum_\lambda \sigma(\lambda) \, \Phi_\text{source}(\lambda) \]

The same emission is then detected by each channel of the track, through its own emission path. A light source shared by several channels of the track is counted once. With the default, tracks="sequential", each channel's \(k\) comes from its own light sources only.

items.title: Excitation saturation
items.text:
A fluorophore that has absorbed a photon cannot absorb another until it returns to the ground state, on average after its fluorescence lifetime \(\tau\). At high irradiance, emission therefore grows more slowly than the excitation. For a two-level system at steady state, the emission rate is proportional to

\[ \frac{k}{1 + k\tau} \]

The product \(s = k\tau\) is the saturation parameter (OpticalConfig.saturation_parameter, for a channel on its own; in a track, \(k\) includes every light source of the track). When \(s \ll 1\), emission is proportional to irradiance. At \(s = 1\) it is half of what a linear response would give.

Emission rate of one molecule against irradiance, uniform over the molecule as in widefield. The rate approaches \(\phi / \tau\), one photon per lifetime times the quantum yield.

How saturation is applied depends on the modality:

  • Widefield: the irradiance is uniform, so the emission rates are reduced by \(1 / (1 + s)\).
  • Confocal: the irradiance varies across the focused spot, so saturation is applied at each position of the excitation PSF. The peak saturates first, which broadens the effective PSF. Here power is the irradiance at the center of the spot, and filtered_emission_rates() gives the (saturated) rates there.

Saturation requires lifetime_ns on the fluorophore. Fluorophores from FPbase usually have one.

Not modeled

Triplet and other dark states, stimulated emission, the orientation of the absorption dipole relative to polarized excitation, and pulsed excitation. With pulsed lasers or with dark-state buildup, real fluorophores saturate at lower average irradiance than this model gives.

items.title: From rates to images
items.text: The emission rate of each fluorophore is per molecule. The next stage multiplies it by the number of fluorophores in each voxel and convolves with the PSF. The widefield PSF is normalized so that each plane sums to about 1: a camera focused at any depth records all the light that the objective collected from a point source. The confocal PSF is scaled by the relative excitation intensity at each position and by the fraction of collected light that passes the pinhole.

items.title: Samples
items.text:
The sample says where fluorophores are and which fluorophores they are. It is a list of labels. Each label combines

  • a distribution: how many fluorophores are in each voxel of the truth space, and
  • a fluorophore: its spectra, brightness, and lifetime.
sample = ms.Sample(
    labels=[
        ms.FluorophoreDistribution(
            distribution=ms.MatsLines(density=0.5),
            fluorophore="EGFP",
        ),
        ms.FluorophoreDistribution(
            distribution=ms.CosemLabel(dataset="jrc_hela-3", label="mito-mem_pred"),
            fluorophore="mCherry",
            concentration=10,
        ),
    ]
)

ground_truth() draws each label into the truth space and stacks them along the f dimension. The values are fluorophores per voxel.

Shorthand

sample also accepts a plain list, and a label can be a bare distribution. These are equivalent:

sample = ms.Sample(labels=[ms.FluorophoreDistribution(distribution=ms.MatsLines())])
sample = [ms.MatsLines()]

A label without a fluorophore gets a placeholder (see below).

items.title: Random lines
items.text:
MatsLines draws randomly oriented, one-voxel-wide line segments, with one fluorophore per voxel. It is quick to compute and useful for testing.

Parameter Effect density number of lines, as a fraction of the X size in voxels (512 voxels × 0.5 = 256 lines) length line length: 1/20 of the field of view, plus a random amount up to length/20 of it azimuth limits the tilt out of the XY plane: larger values give flatter lines max_r lines are only drawn inside an ellipsoid of this relative radius (1 = touching the edges)

Maximum projections of MatsLines ground truths in a 64 × 256 × 256 truth space, with the defaults (density=1, length=10, azimuth=10, max_r=0.9) and with one parameter changed at a time.

items.title: OpenOrganelle (COSEM)
items.text:
CosemLabel uses segmentations of organelles from FIB-SEM volumes of cells, published by Janelia's COSEM project at OpenOrganelle. These give realistic shapes for the endoplasmic reticulum, mitochondria, nuclear envelope, microtubules, and more.

ms.CosemLabel(dataset="jrc_hela-3", label="er-mem_pred")
  • dataset is the dataset ID from the OpenOrganelle website (e.g. jrc_hela-3, jrc_cos7-11).
  • label is the name of a segmentation or prediction layer in that dataset (e.g. er-mem_pred, mito-mem_pred, ne_pred), or its description.
  • position (optional) shifts the region to extract: the dataset's origin is moved to position (in voxels of the resolution level that is read), and the region around 0 is extracted. By default the region is centered in the dataset.

The data are downloaded on first use and cached. This needs the cosem extra and network access.

Three labels each from two OpenOrganelle datasets (HeLa and macrophage cells), on a 64 nm grid: one plane of the ground truth (left) and of the widefield optical image (right), each label in its own color. In widefield, the top and bottom of the nuclear envelope (cyan) blur into the plane, and fill the nucleus.

Voxel size

The source data are stored at 4 nm voxels and at a series of 2× downsampled levels (8, 16, 32 nm, ...). microsim reads the level that matches the truth space without interpolating, so use the same scale on all three axes, equal to 4 nm times a power of two (e.g. scale=0.064).

items.title: Allen Institute neurons
items.text:
microsim.allen fetches neuron reconstructions from the Allen Cell Types Database and renders them as a 3D mask, which can be used as a fixed array:

from microsim.allen import NeuronReconstruction

mask = NeuronReconstruction.fetch(638976782).binary_mask(voxel_size=1)  # (Z, Y, X)

Reconstruction 638976782 rendered at 1 µm voxels (maximum projections).

Not yet practical at optical resolution

binary_mask renders the whole neuron, hundreds of micrometers across, in one array, and the line widths it draws do not scale with voxel_size.
