At the 50 nm voxels that a simulation needs, the array would be far too large. For now, use it at about 1 µm to explore the morphology, or crop and resample the mask yourself.

items.title: Your own array
items.text:
If you already have a ground truth as an array, for example from a segmentation, pass it directly with Simulation.from_ground_truth:

sim = ms.Simulation.from_ground_truth(
    my_array,  # (Z, Y, X), fluorophores per voxel
    scale=(0.04, 0.02, 0.02),  # voxel size in µm
    output_space={"downscale": 4},
    modality=ms.Confocal(),
)

This creates a truth space with the array's shape and a single label with the placeholder fluorophore. To choose the fluorophore, or to combine several arrays, build the labels yourself with a "fixed-array" distribution:

sim = ms.Simulation(
    truth_space={"shape": nuclei.shape, "scale": (0.04, 0.02, 0.02)},
    sample=[
        {
            "distribution": {"type": "fixed-array", "array": nuclei},
            "fluorophore": "mTagBFP2",
        },
        {
            "distribution": {"type": "fixed-array", "array": actin},
            "fluorophore": "EGFP",
        },
    ],
)

Each array must have exactly the shape of the truth space.

The own ground truth tutorial has a complete example.

items.title: Your own generator
items.text:
Any object with a render(space, xp) method can be used as a distribution. space is an all-zero xarray.DataArray with the shape and coordinates of the truth space; return it with your fluorophore counts added:

import numpy as np
from microsim import schema as ms


class PointSources:
    """Single-voxel emitters at random positions."""

    def __init__(self, n: int = 100, fluors_per_point: int = 500):
        self.n = n
        self.fluors_per_point = fluors_per_point

    def render(self, space, xp=None):
        idx = tuple(np.random.randint(0, s, self.n) for s in space.shape)
        data = np.zeros(space.shape, dtype=space.dtype)
        np.add.at(data, idx, self.fluors_per_point)
        return space + data


sample = [
    ms.FluorophoreDistribution(distribution=PointSources(), fluorophore="mCherry")
]

Each emitter here occupies a single voxel of the truth space, so it is a true point source, much smaller than the PSF. Fluorescent beads are often 100 nm or larger, not much smaller than the PSF; to simulate those, fill a sphere of voxels for each bead instead (as with the shells in the own ground truth tutorial).

With the NumPy backend, np.random is seeded from Settings.random_seed before rendering, so this example is reproducible. Generators like this cannot be saved to JSON. To make one that can, subclass BaseDistribution (a pydantic model).

Contributions welcome

Realistic ground truth makes for realistic simulations. If you write a generator others could use, please open a pull request.

items.title: Fluorophores
items.text:
The simplest way to choose a fluorophore is by name. The spectra, extinction coefficient, quantum yield, and lifetime are then loaded from FPbase:

ms.FluorophoreDistribution(distribution=..., fluorophore="mNeonGreen")

Any fluorescent protein or dye on FPbase with spectra can be used. The name must match the name FPbase displays (case doesn't matter, but other spellings don't work: "Alexa Fluor 488", not "AF488"); the error message suggests the closest match. This needs network access the first time.

To define a fluorophore yourself, give its spectra and photophysical properties:

ms.Fluorophore(
    name="MyDye",
    excitation_spectrum=ms.Spectrum(wavelength=wl_ex, intensity=ex),  # nm, any scale
    emission_spectrum=ms.Spectrum(wavelength=wl_em, intensity=em),
    extinction_coefficient=80_000,  # M⁻¹ cm⁻¹, at the excitation peak
    quantum_yield=0.6,
    lifetime_ns=3.5,
)

What each property does:

Property Used for excitation_spectrum the shape of the absorption spectrum; it is normalized to 1 at its peak extinction_coefficient scales the absorption spectrum to an absorption cross section; required quantum_yield the fraction of absorbed photons that are emitted (treated as 1 if not set) emission_spectrum the distribution of emitted photons over wavelength; normalized to unit sum lifetime_ns excitation saturation; no saturation if not set bleaching_half_life_s not used yet

items.title: The placeholder fluorophore
items.text: A label without a fluorophore uses mockFluorophore: flat excitation and emission spectra from 300 to 799 nm, an extinction coefficient of 50,000 M⁻¹ cm⁻¹, a quantum yield of 1, and a 1 ns lifetime. It is excited by any light source and passes any emission filter. Use it for testing; for realistic brightness, color, and bleedthrough, use a real fluorophore.

items.title: Concentration
items.text:
concentration scales a label's distribution. A number multiplies it, so concentration=10 puts ten fluorophores wherever the distribution had one. A function receives the rendered distribution and returns a new one, for example to add labeling variability:

def patchy(truth):
    rng = np.random.default_rng()
    return truth * rng.poisson(5, size=truth.shape)


ms.FluorophoreDistribution(distribution=..., fluorophore="EGFP", concentration=patchy)

What the values of a distribution mean depends on the distribution:

  • MatsLines puts one fluorophore in each voxel of a line (more where lines cross).
  • CosemLabel with a segmentation layer (names ending in _seg) gives the number of labeled 4 nm source voxels inside each truth voxel: up to 4096 in a 64 nm voxel. With a prediction layer (names ending in _pred), it gives the stored 8-bit prediction score (0–255) at the matching resolution level. Neither is a number of fluorophores.

So the brightness of a simulation depends strongly on the distribution and the voxel size, and concentration is how you bring the labeling density in line with your experiment. For scale: an EGFP molecule is a barrel about 4.2 nm long and 2.4 nm wide (Yang, Moss & Phillips 1996), about 19 nm³. Even a 10 nm voxel (1000 nm³) could hold only about 50 of them packed solid, and a 64 nm voxel about 14,000. Real labeled structures are much sparser than that: often hundreds to thousands of fluorophores per cubic micrometer.

items.title: Caching
items.text: Generating some ground truths is slow (CosemLabel downloads data), so MatsLines and CosemLabel results are cached on disk, keyed by their parameters, the truth space, the concentration, and (for random distributions) the random seed. See Settings to clear or disable the cache.

items.title: Saving the result
items.text:
Set output_path and run() writes the digital image to disk:

sim = ms.Simulation(..., output_path="result.zarr")
sim.run()
Extension Format Stores the simulation parameters Requires .zarr Zarr yes .nc NetCDF yes .tif, .tiff TIFF no (pixel data only) io extra

Zarr and NetCDF files keep the dimension names, coordinates (µm), and channel names, and store the full simulation as JSON in the microsim.Simulation attribute. Open them with xarray:

import xarray as xr

result = xr.open_dataarray("result.zarr", engine="zarr")
sim = ms.Simulation.model_validate_json(result.attrs["microsim.Simulation"])

Prefer Zarr

Without the netCDF4 package installed, xarray writes NetCDF files in the older NetCDF-3 format, which has no unsigned integer types. Writing a 16-bit image with gray values above 32,767 fails with a ValueError. Zarr has no such limit.

To save intermediate stages, use xarray directly, for example sim.optical_image().to_netcdf("optical.nc").

items.title: Saving the simulation
items.text:
A Simulation is a pydantic model, so it can be written to and read from JSON:

from pathlib import Path

Path("sim.json").write_text(sim.model_dump_json(indent=2))

sim = ms.Simulation.model_validate_json(Path("sim.json").read_text())

The JSON is complete: fluorophores loaded from FPbase are saved with their spectra, so loading does not need network access (except for a CosemLabel sample, which queries OpenOrganelle when it is loaded). It also includes the random seed, so loading and running the simulation in the same environment reproduces the result.

You can also write simulations as JSON (or YAML, or anything that loads into a dictionary) by hand. Only the fields you want to change from the defaults are needed:

confocal.json
{
  "truth_space": {"shape": [128, 512, 512], "scale": [0.02, 0.01, 0.01]},
  "output_space": {"downscale": 8},
  "sample": [
    {"distribution": {"type": "matslines", "density": 0.5, "length": 30}, "fluorophore": "EGFP"}
  ],
  "channels": ["wKqWbg::Widefield Green"],
  "modality": {"type": "confocal", "pinhole_au": 0.5},
  "detector": {"camera_type": "CMOS", "qe": 0.8, "read_noise": 1.5},
  "settings": {"random_seed": 42},
  "output_path": "confocal.zarr"
}

What cannot be serialized

Custom distribution objects (a class with a render method that is not a pydantic model) and functions used as concentration cannot be written to JSON. When writing the output file, microsim then stores the simulation without the sample.

Record the version

A saved simulation describes the parameters, not the implementation. microsim is changing quickly: a newer version may reject a saved JSON file, or produce a different image from it. Keep microsim.__version__ with your saved simulations and results.

items.title: Settings
items.text:
Settings holds options that affect how a simulation is computed, but not what it represents.

sim = ms.Simulation(..., settings=ms.Settings(random_seed=42, np_backend="jax"))
Setting Default Effect random_seed random seed for the ground truth and noise np_backend "auto" array library used for computation float_dtype float32 floating-point precision max_psf_radius_aus "auto" lateral size limit of each PSF, in Airy radii spectral_bins_per_emission_channel 1 number of PSFs used per fluorophore and channel excitation_bin_width_nm 10 widest band of excitation light given one excitation spot spectral_bin_threshold_percentage 1 part of the spectra that is ignored when binning cache on read and write the on-disk ground-truth cache

items.title: Reproducibility
items.text:
Random numbers are used to generate some ground truths (such as MatsLines) and to draw every kind of noise. When the Simulation is created without a random_seed, a random one is chosen. It is stored on the object, so sim.settings.random_seed tells you which seed was used, and saving the simulation to JSON records it.

With a fixed seed, the same simulation run twice in the same environment gives the same result. Different backends use different random number generators, so results are not identical across backends.

Reproducing results across versions

microsim is under active development, and the same parameters and seed may give different results in a different version of microsim, as models are corrected and extended. Record the version (microsim.__version__) with your results, and pin it in your environment.

items.title: Array backends
items.text:
Computation is done with NumPy by default. Most of the time goes into PSF calculation and FFT convolution, which can run on a GPU:

np_backend Library "numpy" NumPy and SciPy (CPU) "cupy" CuPy (NVIDIA GPU) "jax" JAX (CPU or GPU) "torch" PyTorch (incomplete) "auto" CuPy if it can be imported, otherwise NumPy

The backend can also be chosen with the MICROSIM_BACKEND environment variable, which is used when np_backend is "auto".

With a GPU backend, the arrays inside the returned DataArray live on the GPU. Use .values or numpy.asarray() to get a NumPy array.

items.title: Accuracy vs. speed
items.text:
max_psf_radius_aus limits the lateral size of each PSF to this many Airy radii from the center. A smaller value makes convolution much faster but drops the faint outer parts of the PSF, which in widefield carry a noticeable fraction of the out-of-focus light. With "auto" (the default), the radius is chosen to keep the error from truncation at or below about 1% (RMSE, relative to an untruncated PSF):

  • Widefield: 14 Airy radii, plus half the radius of the cone of out-of-focus light at half the depth of the truth space. At 1.4 NA and 525 nm, this is about 17 Airy radii for a 1 µm deep volume and 27 for 5 µm.
  • Confocal: 8 Airy radii, because the pinhole rejects most out-of-focus light.

A number sets the radius directly. None uses PSFs as large as the truth space. The PSF is never larger than the truth space.

spectral_bins_per_emission_channel sets how many wavelengths are used to represent each fluorophore's detected emission. With 1 (the default), one PSF at the centroid wavelength is used. With more, the emission spectrum (after dropping the parts below spectral_bin_threshold_percentage of its peak) is split into that many bins, and one PSF is computed per bin and weighted by its photons. Time and memory grow with the number of bins.

excitation_bin_width_nm applies to modalities with a focused excitation spot (Confocal). The light each fluorophore absorbs (after dropping the parts below spectral_bin_threshold_percentage of its peak) is grouped into bins at most this wide, and one excitation spot is computed per bin, weighted by the light absorbed in it. A single laser line gives one spot, and laser lines further apart than this are always computed separately. A broadband source gives one spot per bin.

float_dtype can be set to float64 for higher precision, at twice the memory.

items.title: Caching
items.text:
microsim caches results that are slow to compute and depend only on their parameters:

  • PSFs, in memory and on disk. Detection PSFs and confocal excitation spots are cached separately (in memory, the most recent 64 of each).
  • Fourier transforms of PSFs, in memory, up to Settings.cache.in_mem_size.otf_mb (1000 MB by default; GPU memory for GPU backends).
  • Emission rates (what filtered_emission_rates is computed from), in memory, for the most recent 32 combinations of channels, tracks, fluorophores, detector QE, and objective.
  • Ground truth from MatsLines and CosemLabel, on disk, keyed by the distribution's parameters, the truth space, and the concentration (and, for random distributions such as MatsLines, the random seed).
  • OpenOrganelle downloads, on disk.

The disk cache is in the user cache directory given by platformdirs (for example ~/Library/Caches/microsim on macOS, ~/.cache/microsim on Linux):

from microsim.util import microsim_cache, clear_cache

microsim_cache()  # path to the cache directory
clear_cache()  # delete everything
clear_cache("psf/*")  # delete matching entries

To turn caching off:

  • Settings(cache=False) disables reading and writing the ground-truth cache. Settings(cache={"read": True, "write": False}) controls the two separately.
  • The environment variable MICROSIM_CACHE=0 disables both the ground-truth and the PSF disk caches.

items.title: Environment variables
items.text:
Every setting can be set with an environment variable named MICROSIM_ followed by the setting name. Nested settings use __ as a separator:

export MICROSIM_RANDOM_SEED=42
export MICROSIM_NP_BACKEND=jax
export MICROSIM_CACHE__WRITE=0   # read the cache, but don't write to it

Values passed in code take precedence over environment variables.

items.title: Spaces
items.text:
A simulation uses two grids:

  • The truth space is where the sample is drawn and the optical image is computed. It should be fine enough to represent the structures in your sample and to sample the PSF well, typically 10–50 nm per voxel.
  • The output space is the pixel grid of the final image, as recorded by the detector. A typical camera pixel, projected onto the sample, is 60–160 nm.

Both have the same physical extent. The optical image is computed in the truth space and then binned down to the output space just before the detector model.

A detail of the overview figure: the optical image on the 64 nm truth grid (left), and the digital image after binning 2 × 2 × 2 to the 128 nm output grid (right).

items.title: Defining a space
items.text:
A space has a shape (number of voxels along Z, Y, X), a scale (voxel size in µm), and an extent (shape × scale). Give any two and the third is computed:

shape and scaleextent and scaleshape and extent 
ms.ShapeScaleSpace(shape=(64, 512, 512), scale=(0.04, 0.02, 0.02))
# dict form:
{"shape": (64, 512, 512), "scale": (0.04, 0.02, 0.02)}

ms.ExtentScaleSpace(extent=(2.56, 10.24, 10.24), scale=(0.04, 0.02, 0.02))
# dict form:
{"extent": (2.56, 10.24, 10.24), "scale": (0.04, 0.02, 0.02)}

ms.ShapeExtentSpace(shape=(64, 512, 512), extent=(2.56, 10.24, 10.24))
# dict form:
{"shape": (64, 512, 512), "extent": (2.56, 10.24, 10.24)}

A single number for scale applies to all axes: scale=0.02 is the same as scale=(0.02, 0.02, 0.02). A space can also be 2D, with a shape of length 2.

items.title: Relative spaces
items.text:
Usually one space is given explicitly and the other is defined relative to it:

# the output pixels are 8x larger than the truth voxels, along every axis
ms.Simulation(
    truth_space={"shape": (128, 512, 512), "scale": (0.02, 0.01, 0.01)},
    output_space={"downscale": 8},  # -> shape (16, 64, 64), scale (0.16, 0.08, 0.08)
    ...
)

# or: start from the image you want, and compute the truth space from it
ms.Simulation(
    truth_space={"upscale": 4},  # -> shape (64, 256, 256), scale (0.04, 0.02, 0.02)
    output_space={"shape": (16, 64, 64), "scale": (0.16, 0.08, 0.08)},
    ...
)

downscale and upscale take one integer for all axes, or one per axis (e.g. {"downscale": (4, 8, 8)}). At most one of the two spaces may be relative.

output_space may be omitted, in which case the digital image has the shape and scale of the truth space.

items.title: How the downsampling works
items.text:
When the optical image is binned into the output space, Y and X are handled differently for cameras and point scanners:

  • A camera pixel collects all the light that falls on its area, so the truth voxels in each output pixel are summed in Y and X.
  • A point scanner records the signal at each scan position, so the truth voxels are averaged. The dwell time, not the pixel area, sets the signal.

In Z, voxels are always averaged: each output plane is a separate exposure at one focal position, and does not collect light from neighboring planes.

As a consequence, changing output_space changes the camera's signal per pixel (larger pixels collect more light) but not the point scanner's.

items.title: Choosing the sizes
items.text:
Guidelines
  • Truth voxel size. The truth grid must resolve the PSF: at 1.4 NA and 500 nm emission the lateral resolution is about 200 nm, so 20–50 nm voxels are adequate for the optics. Finer voxels are needed only to represent fine structure in the sample itself.
  • Integer ratio. The output scale should be an integer multiple of the truth scale along each axis.
  • Memory and time. The truth space dominates both. A 128 × 1024 × 1024 float32 volume is 512 MB, and the simulation holds several arrays of this size (one per fluorophore and channel) at once. Start small and increase the size when the parameters are right.
  • PSF size. The lateral size of the PSF is limited by Settings.max_psf_radius_aus, so a large field of view does not make each PSF larger.
  • Edges. The convolution treats everything outside the volume as empty. Light from structures just outside the field of view is missing, and the top and bottom planes have less out-of-focus light than they would in a thicker sample.

Camera pixel size and magnification

The output pixel size is set directly by output_space. The camera's physical pixel size and the objective's magnification are not used yet. For a camera with 6.5 µm pixels behind a 60× objective, set the output scale to 6.5 / 60 ≈ 0.108 µm.

items.title: Tutorials
items.text:
Longer worked examples. Each one builds a complete simulation and explains the choices along the way. Each is also a Jupyter notebook: open it in Google Colab to run it without installing anything, or download it. The figures on these pages are made by running the code shown.

  • Two-color imaging of a cell

    Realistic ground truth from OpenOrganelle, fluorophores and filter sets from FPbase, and every step of the photon budget plotted. Widefield, then confocal.

  • Using your own ground truth

    Simulate any 3D array of fluorophore counts, in widefield and confocal.

  • Point-scanning detectors

    PMT high voltage and clipping, photon counting with a HyD, and line averaging, on one confocal image.

More examples are in the examples/ folder of the repository.

items.title: Point-scanning detectors
items.text:
Google Colab Open in Colab Download notebook

This tutorial compares a photomultiplier tube (PMT) and a hybrid detector (HyD) on the same confocal image. It shows how the PMT high voltage trades signal against clipping, and how photon counting and line averaging affect noise. The complete script is examples/point_detectors.py.

items.title: The confocal simulation
items.text:
A single confocal plane of random lines labeled with EGFP, with 80 nm pixels:

from microsim import schema as ms
from microsim.schema.detectors import lib
from microsim.schema.optical_config.lib import LASER_488

sim = ms.Simulation(
    truth_space={"upscale": 4},
    output_space=ms.ShapeScaleSpace(shape=(1, 128, 128), scale=(0.16, 0.08, 0.08)),
    sample=[
        ms.FluorophoreDistribution(
            distribution=ms.MatsLines(density=0.5, length=30, azimuth=5, max_r=1),
            fluorophore="EGFP",
        )
    ],
    channels=[LASER_488.model_copy(update={"power": 2e4})],  # (1)!
    modality=ms.Confocal(pinhole_au=1),
    settings=ms.Settings(random_seed=100),
    detector=lib.HYD_SP8,  # (2)!
)
optical_image = sim.optical_image()
  1. A 488 nm laser with a 525/50 emission filter, at 20 kW/cm² at the focus (about 10 µW at 1.4 NA; the library default is 100 kW/cm²). The brightest pixels receive tens of millions of photons per second. EGFP is only slightly saturated at this irradiance (\(k\tau \approx 0.03\)).
  2. The detector's QE is applied when the optical image is computed. All the detectors compared below have GaAsP photocathodes with nearly identical QE spectra, so one optical image serves for all of them.

items.title: Four detector settings
items.text:
digital_image accepts an existing optical image and an exposure time, so each detector only repeats the last stage. For a point scanner, exposure_ms is the pixel dwell time; here 1 µs.

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

detectors = {
    "GaAsP PMT, 0.7 V": lib.PMT_GAASP.model_copy(update={"hv": 0.7}),
    "GaAsP PMT, 0.9 V": lib.PMT_GAASP.model_copy(update={"hv": 0.9}),
    "HyD (counting)": lib.HYD_SP8,
    "HyD, 4× averaging": lib.HYD_SP8.model_copy(update={"averaging": 4}),
}

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 4, figsize=(13, 3.8))
for ax, (name, detector) in zip(axes, detectors.items()):
    sim.detector = detector
    img = sim.digital_image(optical_image, exposure_ms=0.001)
    ax.imshow(img[0, 0], cmap="gray")
    ax.set_title(f"{name}\nmax gray value: {int(img.max())}")
    ax.axis("off")

What to notice:

  • PMT high voltage. hv is the control voltage of a Hamamatsu photosensor module, 0.5–0.9 V. At 0.7 V the brightest pixels stay below the 12-bit maximum of 4095. At 0.9 V the gain is about 5 times higher, and many pixels clip. Raising the HV barely changes the signal-to-noise ratio of the photon signal, which is set by the number of photoelectrons; it scales the signal up relative to the amplifier noise and the digitization step.
  • Photon counting. The HyD reports photon counts directly (the maximum here is a few dozen), with no gain noise and no read noise. For the same photons its images are less noisy than the PMT's, mainly because the PMT's dynode gain is random (excess noise factor about 1.3).
  • Averaging. With averaging=4, each line is scanned four times and the counts are averaged. The brightness stays the same, and the noise falls by about a factor of 2.

items.title: Going further
items.text: The PMT model also includes output-current saturation (max_output_current_ua, set in the library presets) and the amplifier's time constant (time_constant_us), which smears signal along the scan direction at short dwell times. The HyD model includes count losses from dead time. See Detectors for the details.

items.title: Two-color imaging of a cell
items.text:
Google Colab Open in Colab Download notebook

This tutorial simulates a widefield image of a HeLa cell with the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) labeled with EGFP and the mitochondria labeled with mCherry. Along the way it plots each step of the photon budget, so you can see where the signal and the crosstalk in each channel come from.

It needs the cosem and view extras (both in microsim[all]) and network access, to download the ground truth from OpenOrganelle and spectra from FPbase.

items.title: A first sample
items.text:
The simplest sample is a set of random lines in a 64 × 256 × 256 volume of 10 nm voxels:

from microsim import schema as ms
from microsim.util import ortho_plot

sim = ms.Simulation(
    truth_space=ms.ShapeScaleSpace(shape=(64, 256, 256), scale=0.01),
    sample=[ms.MatsLines()],
)

ortho_plot(sim.ground_truth(), mip=True)

ortho_plot shows XY, XZ, and YZ views, either through the center of the volume or (with mip=True) as maximum projections.

items.title: Realistic ground truth from OpenOrganelle
items.text:
OpenOrganelle publishes FIB-SEM volumes of whole cells, with organelles segmented at 4–8 nm resolution. CosemLabel turns a segmentation layer into a ground truth. Here we use the ER membrane and mitochondrial membrane predictions from cell jrc_hela-3, on a 64 nm grid:

sim = ms.Simulation(
    truth_space=ms.ShapeScaleSpace(shape=(64, 512, 512), scale=(0.064, 0.064, 0.064)),
    sample=[
        ms.CosemLabel(dataset="jrc_hela-3", label="er-mem_pred"),
        ms.CosemLabel(dataset="jrc_hela-3", label="mito-mem_pred"),
    ],
)

ortho_plot(sim.ground_truth(), z=18)

Or as maximum projections:

ortho_plot(sim.ground_truth(), mip=True)

items.title: The optical image
items.text:
With no other configuration, the simulation uses a widefield microscope with a 1.4 NA objective and a FITC filter set:

ortho_plot(sim.optical_image(), z=18)

This looks like a widefield image of a cell, but the ER and mitochondria appear together in the one channel. Neither label has a fluorophore, so both use the placeholder fluorophore, which is excited by any light and passes any filter.

items.title: Fluorophores and channels
items.text:
Next we give each label a fluorophore and define two channels. The fluorophore properties come from FPbase, and so do the two channels: the "Widefield Green" and "Widefield Red" configurations of the Example Simple Widefield microscope, which use an LED light source and Semrock filters.

sim = ms.Simulation(
    truth_space=ms.ShapeScaleSpace(shape=(64, 512, 512), scale=(0.064, 0.064, 0.064)),
    sample=[
        ms.FluorophoreDistribution(
            distribution=ms.CosemLabel(dataset="jrc_hela-3", label="er-mem_pred"),
            fluorophore="EGFP",
        ),
        ms.FluorophoreDistribution(
            distribution=ms.CosemLabel(dataset="jrc_hela-3", label="mito-mem_pred"),
            fluorophore="mCherry",
        ),
    ],
    channels=[
        ms.OpticalConfig.from_fpbase(
            microscope_id="wKqWbg", config_name="Widefield Green"
        ),
        ms.OpticalConfig.from_fpbase(
            microscope_id="wKqWbg", config_name="Widefield Red"
        ),
    ],
)

How many photons a fluorophore contributes to a channel depends on two overlaps: between its absorption spectrum and the excitation light, and between its emission spectrum and the emission filters and detector. The next sections follow the photons through both. The Photon budget page has the equations.

items.title: Absorption
items.text:
from matplotlib import pyplot as plt

plt.figure(figsize=(12, 4))
for lbl in sim.sample.labels:
    fluor = lbl.fluorophore
    fluor.absorption_cross_section.plot.line(label=fluor.name)
plt.legend()

The excitation spectra from FPbase, scaled by each fluorophore's extinction coefficient and converted to an absorption cross section in cm² per molecule.

items.title: Excitation light
items.text:
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, len(sim.channels), figsize=(12, 3))
for ax, oc in zip(axes, sim.channels):
    oc.plot_excitation(ax=ax)

The colored lines are the LED spectrum and the excitation-side filters (right-hand scale, relative). The black line is the photon flux reaching the sample (left-hand scale, photons/cm²/s). The channel's power is not set, so the total irradiance is the default 1 W/cm². Change it with oc.power = <W/cm²>.

items.title: Absorption rate
items.text:
The product of cross section and photon flux is the absorption rate: photons absorbed per second, per molecule.

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, len(sim.channels), figsize=(12, 3))
for ax, oc in zip(axes, sim.channels):
    for lbl in sim.sample.labels:
        abs_rate = oc.absorption_rate(lbl.fluorophore)
        abs_rate.plot(
            ax=ax, label=f"{lbl.fluorophore.name} ({abs_rate.sum():.0f} photons/s)"
        )
    ax.set_xlim(400, 700)
    ax.legend(loc="center right")
    ax.set_title(oc.name)

EGFP is excited mostly by the green channel and mCherry by the red one. The green channel also excites mCherry a little (21 vs. 530 photons/s): this is cross-excitation, one source of crosstalk.

items.title: Emission
items.text:
Each absorbed photon is re-emitted with a probability equal to the quantum yield, with wavelengths distributed according to the emission spectrum:

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, len(sim.channels), figsize=(12, 3))
for ax, oc in zip(axes, sim.channels):
    for lbl in sim.sample.labels:
        fluor = lbl.fluorophore
        em_rate = oc.total_emission_rate(fluor)
        em_rate.plot(
            ax=ax,
            label=f"{fluor.name} (QY: {fluor.quantum_yield}) ({em_rate.sum():.0f} photons/s)",
        )
    ax.set_xlim(400, 800)
    ax.legend(fontsize=8)
    ax.set_title(oc.name)

items.title: Emission path
items.text:
The emitted light then passes the dichroic and emission filter. Their combined transmission (black) selects the light that reaches the detector:

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, len(sim.channels), figsize=(12, 3))
for ax, oc in zip(axes, sim.channels):
    oc.plot_emission(ax=ax)

items.title: Detected photons
items.text:
Multiplying the emission rate by the transmission of the emission path gives the photons per second that pass the filters, for each fluorophore in each channel:

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, len(sim.channels), figsize=(12, 3))
for ax, oc in zip(axes, sim.channels):
    for lbl in sim.sample.labels:
        fluor = lbl.fluorophore
        oc.total_emission_rate(fluor).plot(ax=ax, color="k", alpha=0.1)
        filtered = oc.filtered_emission_rate(fluor)
        filtered.plot(ax=ax, label=f"{fluor.name} ({filtered.sum():.0f} photons/s)")
    ax.set_xlim(400, 800)
    ax.legend(fontsize=8)
    ax.set_title(oc.name)

Collection efficiency

These per-channel plots assume that every emitted photon reaches the filters. In the simulation, the rates are also multiplied by the fraction of light the objective collects, about 35% for this 1.4 NA objective, and, if a detector is set, by its QE. sim.filtered_emission_rates() returns the rates with these applied. See Photon budget.

items.title: The optical image, again
items.text:
Now each fluorophore's light is assigned to the channels in proportion to the rates above:

ortho_plot(sim.optical_image(), z=18)

items.title: Detector and pixels
items.text:
To get a digital image we add a detector, which determines the noise, and an output space, which sets the pixel size. Here, the ICX285 CCD and pixels twice the size of the truth voxels (128 nm):

sim.detector = ms.detectors.lib.ICX285
sim.output_space = ms.DownscaledSpace(downscale=2)

ortho_plot(sim.digital_image(exposure_ms=100), z=9)

With a ten times shorter exposure, there are ten times fewer photons, and the shot noise and read noise are more visible:

ortho_plot(sim.digital_image(exposure_ms=10), z=9)

Raising the illumination to 10 W/cm² brings the signal back:

sim.channels[0].power = 10
sim.channels[1].power = 10
ortho_plot(sim.digital_image(exposure_ms=10), z=9)

items.title: Confocal
items.text:
Changing the modality to Confocal removes most of the out-of-focus light. For a point-scanning modality, power is the peak irradiance at the focus of the laser spot and exposure_ms is the dwell time per pixel, so both are set to typical confocal values:

sim.modality = ms.Confocal(pinhole_au=1)
sim.channels[0].power = 5_000  # W/cm² at the focus
sim.channels[1].power = 5_000

ortho_plot(sim.digital_image(exposure_ms=0.01), z=9)  # 10 µs pixel dwell

The channels still use the LED spectrum from the widefield configuration; only the irradiance and the PSF changed. For laser excitation, use the laser lines in lib (e.g. LASER_488). The detector is still the CCD camera; point-scanning confocals record with point detectors, as in point-scanning detectors.

items.title: Using your own ground truth
items.text:
Google Colab Open in Colab Download notebook

If you already have a 3D array that describes your sample (a segmentation, a mesh you voxelized, or shapes you generated), you can simulate it directly.

items.title: Make an array
items.text:
The array holds the number of fluorophores in each voxel. Here: a dozen hollow spherical shells with random centers and radii, ten fluorophores per voxel of shell.

import numpy as np

shape = (64, 256, 256)  # Z, Y, X
z, y, x = np.ogrid[: shape[0], : shape[1], : shape[2]]
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)

truth = np.zeros(shape, dtype=np.float32)
for _ in range(12):
    cz, cy, cx = rng.integers(16, 48), rng.integers(30, 226), rng.integers(30, 226)
    r = rng.integers(8, 28)
    # distance from the center; Z voxels are twice as large as Y and X
    d = np.sqrt(((z - cz) * 2) ** 2 + (y - cy) ** 2 + (x - cx) ** 2)
    truth += (np.abs(d - r) < 1.5) * 10

items.title: Simulate it
items.text:
Simulation.from_ground_truth takes the array and its voxel size in µm, plus any other simulation parameters:

from microsim import schema as ms
from microsim.schema.optical_config import lib

common = dict(
    scale=(0.04, 0.02, 0.02),  # voxel size of the array, in µm
    output_space={"downscale": 4},  # 160 x 80 x 80 nm pixels
    detector=ms.CameraCMOS(qe=0.8, read_noise=1.5),
    settings=ms.Settings(random_seed=0),
)

widefield = ms.Simulation.from_ground_truth(truth, **common).run()

confocal = ms.Simulation.from_ground_truth(
    truth,
    modality=ms.Confocal(),
    channels=[lib.LASER_488.model_copy(update={"power": 5000})],  # W/cm² at focus
    exposure_ms=0.01,  # 10 µs dwell
    **common,
).run()

Plot one plane of each. The digital images have dimensions (c, z, y, x), and their 16 Z planes cover the 64 planes of the array:

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

panels = {
    "your array (z = 32)": truth[32],
    "widefield": widefield[0, 8],
    "confocal": confocal[0, 8],
}
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(11, 4))
for ax, (title, image) in zip(axes, panels.items()):
    ax.imshow(image, cmap="gray")
    ax.set_title(title)
    ax.axis("off")

The widefield image shows rings from shells centered above and below this plane as blurred discs. The confocal image rejects most of that light.

items.title: Choosing a fluorophore
items.text:
from_ground_truth uses the placeholder fluorophore. To use a real one, or to combine several arrays as separate labels, use a "fixed-array" distribution:

sim = ms.Simulation(
    truth_space={"shape": truth.shape, "scale": (0.04, 0.02, 0.02)},
    sample=[
        {
            "distribution": {"type": "fixed-array", "array": truth},
            "fluorophore": "mScarlet",
        }
    ],
    channels=[lib.TRITC],
)

Every array must have the shape of the truth space.

items.title: Things to keep in mind
items.text:
• Values are fluorophore counts. A binary mask gives one fluorophore per voxel, which is usually very dim. Scale the array to a realistic labeling density (see Concentration).
  • Voxel size. The array should be sampled finely enough for the optics: 50 nm or less laterally for a high-NA objective. If your data are coarser, upsample them first.
  • Anisotropy. scale can differ between axes, as here, where Z voxels are twice as large.
  • Identity modality. If your array is already a microscope image and you only want the spectral and detector parts of the simulation, use modality=ms.Identity(), which skips the PSF.
